items.fromString:
h1. Feature: Deployment of RHOSO 18 on OpenShift Version 4.22

h2. Overview

RHOSO 18 supports only LTS (Extended Update Support) versions of OpenShift Container Platform (OCP). As OCP 4.22 becomes the next LTS release, RHOSO 18 must be qualified, shipped, and documented against it. This feature captures the full scope of work required to make OCP 4.22 a supported platform for RHOSO 18, from production chain updates through CI coverage and customer documentation.

RelDel owns the delivery side of this effort: updating the OLM bundle and update graph to include OCP 4.22, coordinating operator migration, and producing the documentation customers need to deploy, upgrade, and operate RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.22. CI and infrastructure teams support by extending test coverage to OCP 4.22 and adding upgrade job support, but the feature's completion gate is the shippable content RelDel produces.

Qualifying OCP 4.22 keeps RHOSO 18 current with Red Hat's supported platform matrix, gives customers a clear upgrade path from OCP 4.20, and positions the product to remain within the OCP EUS support window through the next feature release cycle.

----

h2. Goals

h3. Technical Objectives

- Update the OLM bundle and index image to include OCP 4.22 as a supported release
- Add and validate the OCP 4.22 update graph, including EUS-to-EUS paths
- Migrate in-scope operators to support OCP 4.22 (openstack-operator, test-operator, watcher, and others as identified)
- Extend CI coverage to include OCP 4.22 deployment and upgrade jobs
- Update customer documentation to reflect OCP 4.22 as the current preferred supported version

h3. Who benefits from this Feature, and how?

- *Customers:* Gain access to RHOSO 18 updates on OCP 4.22, the newest LTS release, with a clear and documented upgrade path from OCP 4.20.
- *Red Hat Engineering:* CI coverage on OCP 4.22 catches regressions early; a validated update graph reduces support escalations at customer upgrade time.
- *Documentation & Support Readiness:* Updated documentation and release notes give support engineers accurate guidance for customers deploying or upgrading to OCP 4.22.
- *Product Delivery:* A complete and validated OLM bundle with OCP 4.22 in the index image allows RHOSO 18 to ship on a current, in-support platform combination.

h3. What is the difference between today's current state and a world with this Feature?

Today, RHOSO 18 does not include OCP 4.22 in its supported platform matrix. Customers who upgrade their OCP clusters to 4.22 will find no RHOSO update path available to them. The OLM bundle and index image do not include 4.22, documentation references OCP 4.20 as the current preferred version, and no CI jobs run against OCP 4.22 infrastructure.

With this feature in place, OCP 4.22 is a fully supported platform for RHOSO 18. Customers can perform greenfield deployments, upgrade from OCP 4.20, and adopt from OSP 17.1 — all on OCP 4.22. The OLM bundle includes 4.22 in the index, the update graph is validated and published, and documentation guides customers through every supported path.

----

h2. Requirements

||Requirement||Notes||isMVP?||
|OLM bundle updated to include OCP 4.22 as a supported release|Bundle must include OCP 4.22 in the index image and advertise compatibility|Yes|
|Update graph added and validated for OCP 4.22|Graph must cover EUS-to-EUS upgrade paths, including the 3-node compact cluster path through 4.21|Yes|
|In-scope operators migrated to support OCP 4.22|Includes openstack-operator, test-operator, watcher, and others identified during scoping|Yes|
|CI framework (CIFMW) updated to support OCP 4.22|Covers unified job support and any framework-level changes required for 4.22 compatibility|Yes|
|Upgrade CI job added from OCP 4.20 EUS to OCP 4.22 EUS|Must cover the compact cluster upgrade path through OCP 4.21|Yes|
|Greenfield deployment validated on OCP 4.22|End-to-end deployment tested and passing in CI|Yes|
|Adoption path validated: OSP 17.1 to RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.22 (FR7)|FR7 is the target milestone; test coverage confirms this path is functional|Yes|
|Documentation updated for OCP 4.22 as the current preferred supported version|Includes {{{ocp_curr_ver}}} variable, updated doc links to the 4.22 path, and lifecycle page updates|Yes|
|Release notes published documenting OCP 4.22 support and upgrade guidance|Customers must know when OCP 4.22 support is available and how to use it|Yes|
|Support matrix documentation updated to include OCP 4.22|Official RHOSO 18 support matrix accurately reflects 4.22 as supported|Yes|

----

h2. Done - Acceptance Criteria

This feature is considered complete when:

# OCP 4.22 is included in the RHOSO 18 OLM index image and customers can install or update RHOSO 18 on an OCP 4.22 cluster using the published catalog.
# The OCP 4.22 update graph is published and validated, including EUS-to-EUS upgrade paths from OCP 4.20 to OCP 4.22.
# CI jobs for OCP 4.22 greenfield deployment are passing, covering the same baseline coverage as OCP 4.20.
# CI jobs for upgrade from OCP 4.20 EUS to OCP 4.22 EUS are passing, including the compact cluster path through OCP 4.21.
# The adoption path from OSP 17.1 to RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.22 is validated in CI by FR7.
# Documentation references OCP 4.22 as the current preferred supported version, with all relevant links and variables updated.
# Release notes for the FR7 milestone document OCP 4.22 support availability and provide upgrade guidance for customers upgrading from OCP 4.20.
# The official RHOSO 18 support matrix includes OCP 4.22.

----

h2. Use Cases

h3. Greenfield Deployment on OCP 4.22

A customer provisions a new OCP 4.22 cluster and deploys RHOSO 18 for the first time. The OLM catalog includes OCP 4.22, operators install without compatibility warnings, and the deployment follows the standard documented path. The customer consults RHOSO documentation that references OCP 4.22 throughout.

h3. EUS-to-EUS Upgrade: OCP 4.20 to OCP 4.22

A customer running RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.20 wants to upgrade their cluster to OCP 4.22. They follow Red Hat's documented EUS upgrade path. The RHOSO update graph supports this transition, and they can continue receiving RHOSO 18 updates without interruption after the upgrade.

h3. Compact Cluster Upgrade (3-Node)

A customer running a 3-node compact cluster on OCP 4.20 needs to upgrade to OCP 4.22. Because OCP does not support a direct 4.20-to-4.22 EUS hop on compact clusters, the customer upgrades OCP 4.20 to 4.21 and then to 4.22. RHOSO 18 remains operational throughout; documentation and release notes describe this path clearly.

h3. Adoption: OSP 17.1 to RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.22

A customer running OSP 17.1 adopts RHOSO 18 at the FR7 milestone. Their target OCP version is 4.22. The adoption path is validated, documented, and confirmed as a supported combination.

h3. Customer Planning Their Upgrade

A customer reads the FR7 release notes during release preparation. The notes document OCP 4.22 support availability, the upgrade path from OCP 4.20, and any platform-level prerequisites. The customer can plan their OCP and RHOSO upgrade together before the next update window.

----

h2. Out of Scope

- OCP non-LTS (odd-numbered) versions — only EUS versions are supported
- Any RHOSO 19 work
- RHOSO 18 support for OCP 4.18 beyond what is already in place — this feature adds 4.22, it does not modify existing support for 4.18 or 4.20
- Infrastructure provisioning for OCP 4.22 CI environments — treated as a dependency owned by the infrastructure team
- Changes to RHOSO 19 operators or delivery pipeline

----

h2. Documentation Considerations

The primary documentation deliverables are:

- Update the {{{ocp_curr_ver}}} variable (and any equivalent) to reflect OCP 4.22 as the current preferred supported version
- Update all documentation links pointing to versioned OCP 4.20 paths to use the 4.22 path
- Update the lifecycle and support matrix pages to list OCP 4.22 as supported
- Publish release notes for the FR7 milestone documenting OCP 4.22 support availability, the supported upgrade paths from OCP 4.20, the compact cluster upgrade sequence (4.20 to 4.21 to 4.22), and the adoption path from OSP 17.1

Documentation should make clear that OCP 4.18 remains supported at FR6, and that customers are not required to upgrade from 4.18 or 4.20 to 4.22 immediately.

----

h2. Questions to Answer

- What is the expected support matrix for Feature Releases vs OpenShift versions at FR6? Specifically: do we support 4.18 through 4.22 at FR6, and is there a plan to drop 4.18 in a subsequent release?
- Are there any changes required to operator-sdk as part of the OCP 4.22 migration?
- What is the exact set of operators that must be migrated to support OCP 4.22 (beyond the known set of openstack-operator, test-operator, and watcher)?
- What needs to happen with the adoption path from OSP 17.1 — are there changes required to documentation or testing frameworks beyond job additions?
- What is the customer communication plan if OCP 4.22 support is not available at the time OCP 4.22 GA ships?

----

h2. Background and Strategic Fit

h3. OCP LTS Cadence and the Two-Release Trailing Rule

RHOSO 18 supports only OCP LTS (EUS) versions. The product commitment is that RHOSO content cannot trail the current LTS by more than two feature releases. OCP 4.22 is expected to be the next LTS release after OCP 4.20. RHOSO 18 must qualify against OCP 4.22 by FR7 to remain within this commitment.

OCP 4.20 support was introduced in FR6. Customers who upgraded to OCP 4.20 at FR6 can upgrade to OCP 4.22 starting from FR7, when OCP 4.22 support becomes available. There is no additional trailing constraint complication for this transition.

h3. Production Chain: FBC Pipeline Already Established

The production chain for OCP 4.22 follows the same File-Based Catalog (FBC) pipeline used for OCP 4.20. There are no new process risks associated with this release cycle — FBC and the Konflux-based build pipeline are already in production use. The work for OCP 4.22 is additive: updating the bundle, extending the update graph, and migrating any operators that have not yet been updated.

h3. Operator Migration Scope

In addition to the main openstack-operator, other operators must be assessed and migrated for each new OCP version: test-operator, watcher, and any additional operators identified during scoping. This coordination effort is a standard part of each OCP LTS qualification cycle.

h3. Upgrade Path Complexity: Compact Clusters

Compact (3-node) clusters do not support a direct OCP 4.20-to-4.22 EUS upgrade. These clusters must traverse OCP 4.21 as an intermediate step (4.20 to 4.21 to 4.22). This is a known platform constraint that must be reflected in CI coverage, the update graph, and customer documentation.

----

h2. Customer Considerations

h3. Upgrade Timing

Customers upgrading from OCP 4.20 to OCP 4.22 should plan to do so at or after FR7, when RHOSO 18 support for OCP 4.22 is available. Upgrading OCP before RHOSO support is available creates a gap in update availability.

h3. Compact Cluster Customers

Customers on 3-node compact clusters must plan for the intermediate OCP 4.21 step. The release notes and documentation will describe this path explicitly.

h3. RHOSO Content Trailing Constraint

OCP 4.20 support was introduced in FR6. Customers on OCP 4.20 can upgrade to OCP 4.22 and roll out the FR7 update once RHOSO 18 support for OCP 4.22 is available. Documentation will clarify the sequencing.

h3. OCP 4.18 Still Supported at FR6

Customers on OCP 4.18 are not required to upgrade to OCP 4.22 at FR6. OCP 4.18 remains within the RHOSO 18 support matrix. Release notes should communicate this clearly to avoid unnecessary urgency.

h3. Adoption Customers

Customers adopting from OSP 17.1 to RHOSO 18 at FR7 should target OCP 4.22. OCP 4.16 support was removed in FR6, so adoption to FR7 with OCP 4.16 is not a supported combination. Adoption with OCP 4.18 or OCP 4.20 remains supported.

----

h2. Team Sign-Off

- All required Epics (known at the time) are linked to this Feature
- All required Stories, Tasks (known at the time) for the most immediate Epics have been created and estimated
- Acceptance means the Feature is "Ready" — well understood with clear scope — and Acceptance Criteria are elaborated, well defined, and understood
- Note: Only set FixVersion/s on a Feature if the delivery team agrees they have the capacity and have committed that capability for that milestone

# The OCP 4.22 update graph is published and validated, including EUS-to-EUS upgrade paths from OCP 4.20 to OCP 4.22.
# CI jobs for OCP 4.22 greenfield deployment are passing, covering the same baseline coverage as OCP 4.20.
# CI jobs for upgrade from OCP 4.20 EUS to OCP 4.22 EUS are passing, including the compact cluster path through OCP 4.21.
# The adoption path from OSP 17.1 to RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.22 is validated in CI by FR7.
# Documentation references OCP 4.22 as the current preferred supported version, with all relevant links and variables updated.
# Release notes for the FR7 milestone document OCP 4.22 support availability and provide upgrade guidance for customers upgrading from OCP 4.20.
# The official RHOSO 18 support matrix includes OCP 4.22.

----

h2. Use Cases

h3. Greenfield Deployment on OCP 4.22

A customer provisions a new OCP 4.22 cluster and deploys RHOSO 18 for the first time. The OLM catalog includes OCP 4.22, operators install without compatibility warnings, and the deployment follows the standard documented path. The customer consults RHOSO documentation that references OCP 4.22 throughout.

h3. EUS-to-EUS Upgrade: OCP 4.20 to OCP 4.22

A customer running RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.20 wants to upgrade their cluster to OCP 4.22. They follow Red Hat's documented EUS upgrade path. The RHOSO update graph supports this transition, and they can continue receiving RHOSO 18 updates without interruption after the upgrade.

h3. Compact Cluster Upgrade (3-Node)

A customer running a 3-node compact cluster on OCP 4.20 needs to upgrade to OCP 4.22. Because OCP does not support a direct 4.20-to-4.22 EUS hop on compact clusters, the customer upgrades OCP 4.20 to 4.21 and then to 4.22. RHOSO 18 remains operational throughout; documentation and release notes describe this path clearly.

h3. Adoption: OSP 17.1 to RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.22

A customer running OSP 17.1 adopts RHOSO 18 at the FR7 milestone. Their target OCP version is 4.22. The adoption path is validated, documented, and confirmed as a supported combination.

h3. Customer Planning Their Upgrade

A customer reads the FR7 release notes during release preparation. The notes document OCP 4.22 support availability, the upgrade path from OCP 4.20, and any platform-level prerequisites. The customer can plan their OCP and RHOSO upgrade together before the next update window.

----

h2. Out of Scope

- OCP non-LTS (odd-numbered) versions — only EUS versions are supported
- Any RHOSO 19 work
- RHOSO 18 support for OCP 4.18 beyond what is already in place — this feature adds 4.22, it does not modify existing support for 4.18 or 4.20
- Infrastructure provisioning for OCP 4.22 CI environments — treated as a dependency owned by the infrastructure team
- Changes to RHOSO 19 operators or delivery pipeline

----

h2. Documentation Considerations

The primary documentation deliverables are:

- Update the {{{ocp_curr_ver}}} variable (and any equivalent) to reflect OCP 4.22 as the current preferred supported version
- Update all documentation links pointing to versioned OCP 4.20 paths to use the 4.22 path
- Update the lifecycle and support matrix pages to list OCP 4.22 as supported
- Publish release notes for the FR7 milestone documenting OCP 4.22 support availability, the supported upgrade paths from OCP 4.20, the compact cluster upgrade sequence (4.20 to 4.21 to 4.22), and the adoption path from OSP 17.1

Documentation should make clear that OCP 4.18 remains supported at FR6, and that customers are not required to upgrade from 4.18 or 4.20 to 4.22 immediately.

----

h2. Questions to Answer

- What is the expected support matrix for Feature Releases vs OpenShift versions at FR6? Specifically: do we support 4.18 through 4.22 at FR6, and is there a plan to drop 4.18 in a subsequent release?
- Are there any changes required to operator-sdk as part of the OCP 4.22 migration?
- What is the exact set of operators that must be migrated to support OCP 4.22 (beyond the known set of openstack-operator, test-operator, and watcher)?
- What needs to happen with the adoption path from OSP 17.1 — are there changes required to documentation or testing frameworks beyond job additions?
- What is the customer communication plan if OCP 4.22 support is not available at the time OCP 4.22 GA ships?

----

h2. Background and Strategic Fit

h3. OCP LTS Cadence and the Two-Release Trailing Rule

RHOSO 18 supports only OCP LTS (EUS) versions. The product commitment is that RHOSO content cannot trail the current LTS by more than two feature releases. OCP 4.22 is expected to be the next LTS release after OCP 4.20. RHOSO 18 must qualify against OCP 4.22 by FR7 to remain within this commitment.

OCP 4.20 support was introduced in FR6. Customers who upgraded to OCP 4.20 at FR6 can upgrade to OCP 4.22 starting from FR7, when OCP 4.22 support becomes available. There is no additional trailing constraint complication for this transition.

h3. Production Chain: FBC Pipeline Already Established

The production chain for OCP 4.22 follows the same File-Based Catalog (FBC) pipeline used for OCP 4.20. There are no new process risks associated with this release cycle — FBC and the Konflux-based build pipeline are already in production use. The work for OCP 4.22 is additive: updating the bundle, extending the update graph, and migrating any operators that have not yet been updated.

h3. Operator Migration Scope

In addition to the main openstack-operator, other operators must be assessed and migrated for each new OCP version: test-operator, watcher, and any additional operators identified during scoping. This coordination effort is a standard part of each OCP LTS qualification cycle.

h3. Upgrade Path Complexity: Compact Clusters

Compact (3-node) clusters do not support a direct OCP 4.20-to-4.22 EUS upgrade. These clusters must traverse OCP 4.21 as an intermediate step (4.20 to 4.21 to 4.22). This is a known platform constraint that must be reflected in CI coverage, the update graph, and customer documentation.

----

h2. Customer Considerations

h3. Upgrade Timing

Customers upgrading from OCP 4.20 to OCP 4.22 should plan to do so at or after FR7, when RHOSO 18 support for OCP 4.22 is available. Upgrading OCP before RHOSO support is available creates a gap in update availability.

h3. Compact Cluster Customers

Customers on 3-node compact clusters must plan for the intermediate OCP 4.21 step. The release notes and documentation will describe this path explicitly.

h3. RHOSO Content Trailing Constraint

OCP 4.20 support was introduced in FR6. Customers on OCP 4.20 can upgrade to OCP 4.22 and roll out the FR7 update once RHOSO 18 support for OCP 4.22 is available. Documentation will clarify the sequencing.

h3. OCP 4.18 Still Supported at FR6

Customers on OCP 4.18 are not required to upgrade to OCP 4.22 at FR6. OCP 4.18 remains within the RHOSO 18 support matrix. Release notes should communicate this clearly to avoid unnecessary urgency.

h3. Adoption Customers

Customers adopting from OSP 17.1 to RHOSO 18 at FR7 should target OCP 4.22. OCP 4.16 support was removed in FR6, so adoption to FR7 with OCP 4.16 is not a supported combination. Adoption with OCP 4.18 or OCP 4.20 remains supported.

----

h2. Team Sign-Off

- All required Epics (known at the time) are linked to this Feature
- All required Stories, Tasks (known at the time) for the most immediate Epics have been created and estimated
- Acceptance means the Feature is "Ready" — well understood with clear scope — and Acceptance Criteria are elaborated, well defined, and understood
- Note: Only set FixVersion/s on a Feature if the delivery team agrees they have the capacity and have committed that capability for that milestone

items.fromString: Cinder Change Block Tracking (CBT) for Backup Solutions
items.toString: Cinder Changed Block Tracking (CBT) for Backup Solutions

items.fromString:
*Feature Overview*

Large-scale OpenStack deployments running enterprise backup and disaster recovery solutions (e.g., Commvault, DRaaS providers) are increasingly constrained by the lack of a backend-agnostic, Change Block Tracking (CBT) capability in OpenStack.

While some storage backends may offer array-specific CBT or replication, customers operating heterogeneous or externally managed storage systems require a neutral mechanism to identify changed blocks at the virtual disk level efficiently. This capability is widely relied upon in VMware-based ecosystems to enable efficient incremental backup and near-continuous replication with low RPO.

This feature will provide a Cinder CBT capability, leveraging existing primitives in storage arrays, to provide a consumable, vendor-neutral foundation for backup and DR integrations.

Cinder would expose a volume CBT API that would in turn call a driver “CBT function“ through the cinder driver’s interface. The driver will use the backend specific capabilities / API to retrieved the list of changed blocks between two snapshots.

The CBT support will therefore be driver specific, each vendor will need to implement it based on their backend capabilities.

*Business Justification*

This feature would enable customers to:

* Perform efficient incremental backups without requiring full volume scans
* Reduce backup windows and backend read I/O for large VM disks
* Support near-continuous DR workflows at the VM level with lower RPO
* Integrate enterprise backup and DR solutions consistently across heterogeneous storage environments
* Achieve parity with expectations set by other virtualization platforms when migrating large-scale workloads to OpenStack

Without a CBT capability, customers face scalability and operational challenges that limit OpenStack adoption for enterprise backup and DR use cases.

*Goals:*

* Deliver software and tests upstream
* Downstream backport changes
* Update customer documentation 
* Downstream automated CI coverage
* Support Enablement

*Requirements*

Backup vendors need a way to query what changed between two different snapshots. The API call should be backend agnostic. Each driver will optionally implement a CBT support function, how the driver interacts with the backend to get the result is specific to the vendor/solution.

The outcome of this feature should be:

# A documented design describing how Cinder can orchestrate volume-level CBT using existing backend capabilities.
# Identification of constraints, limitations, and failure scenarios relevant to backup and DR integrations.
# An architectural analysis of Cinder volume service and cinder drivers interactions interactions required to support CBT in a safe and scalable manner.
# Alignment with upstream OpenStack architectural principles and service boundaries.
# Add certification tests so partners can certify this feature and the capability can be highlighted in the driver certification page

*Done - Acceptance Criteria*

* Deliver feature in RHOSO with customer documentation and downstream automated regression coverage.

*Out of Scope*

* Vendor’s driver’s implementation

*Documentation Considerations*

This is a major new feature that will require storage specific documentation. Documentation persona will primarily targets backup software vendors.

*Prod/CI/RelDel Considerations*

TBD

*Questions to Answer:*

* Which driver’s Red Hat needs to implement.

items.fromString:
*Feature Overview* 

Investigating cluster synchronization issues, split-brain scenarios, and state transfer (SST/IST) failures in MariaDB Galera is currently hindered by transient or fragmented console logs. This feature flips the switch to *enable dedicated Galera logging to disk by default*.

To prevent these logs from consuming unbounded disk space, this feature also introduces a managed *cronjob to handle automated log rotation*.

*Goals* 


* *SRE/Support teams :* They benefit from immediate access to post-mortem data. They no longer have to guess what caused a cluster partition or attempt to "reproduce and capture" a transient replication failure after the node has already crashed.
* *Pidone Team:* They benefit from the automated {{logrotate}} implementation. They are protected against unexpected file system exhaustion or disk-space alerts, as log sizes and retention windows are tightly capped.

*Feature Request Overview (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
_What user goal or problem do you need to solve?_

Today, EDPM images are built using {{diskimage-builder}}, which has a large set of dependencies. This is done because on OSO18 and prior, the images utilize {{os-net-config}} to manage network configurations. Were a customer to need to customize the image, they would need to download our prebuilt image, then alter using e.g. {{virt-customize}} or some other set of tools.

With OSO19, it is my understanding that {{os-net-config}} is no longer required to exist inside our images. Without OpenStack content inside of them, these images only now contain RHEL content and various configuration file changes.

As an alternative for EDPM images, we could consider providing templates for modifying the RHEL Guest Image (using perhaps Ansible roles) or, more simply (and the point of this RFE) providing an OpenStack-specific set of blueprints and documentation in order for customers to leverage [the RHEL Image Builder|https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/composing_a_customized_rhel_system_image/index] during the normal course of deploying an OSO19 environment.

*Business justification (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
_How would this feature benefit the customer?_

Customers are now able to build customized EDPM images that match their requirements using native RHEL10 tools.

*Functional requirements (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
_What do you want the result of this feature to be? Add as many requirements as needed._

* Instead of distributing a pre-built EDPM image, customers are empowered to build an image for their specific environment.
* Image can be reused by customers across their installations
* Documentation illustrates specific requirements so that the resulting EDPM images are usable, including, but not limited to:
** RHEL packages required for use,
** RHEL version(s) and repositories which are supported
** Any required network configuration settings

Additionally Lightspeed stack itself can also accommodate the ability to deploy multiple models within a single “deployment stack” today and has settings for a default inference provider and model.

*Initiative Overview* 

Our RHOSO-18 support for DR partners will require some engineering testing in collaboration with the leading DR partner and our join certified cinder partner.  This initiative captures the supporting work needed to enable that Partner led software solution. 

We have removed the public [Tech Preview of Cinder Replication for DR|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOSSTRAT-903] partners and this initiative replaces that general feature which is moving to a 19-based release.

*Goals*

* Provide an replication hardware setup with target storage partner inside of RH to provide to DR vendor for validation of the solution
* Minor updates to our RHOSO docs to modify the restriction note on use of cinder replication

*Dependencies*

* We require a min of 2 vendor storage arrays for MVP test enviornment
* For any form of scale testing, the Software-based virtual vendor array will be required
* For significant scale testing, the RH perf/scale lab will be required and an approved

*Acceptance Criteria*

* Minor doc changes delivered into RHOSO-18
* Best effort to provide a test environment if Storage vendor dependencies are met)

*Out of Scope*

* This effort is only for 1 specific DR vendor and 1 specific Cinder vendor, this initiative does not cover any other cinder replication or DR vendor efforts

*Open Questions:*

#

items.toString:
h1. Keystone Integration with OpenShift -- Feature Description

See section 5 for the quick “what are we supposed to do” only.

----

h2. 1. Executive Summary

Keystone integration with OpenShift eliminates the identity management gap that has persisted since the transition from OSP 17.1 (TripleO) to RHOSO 18.0 (operator-based). Today, RHOSO customers who need external identity provider (IdP) support, EntraID, ADFS, Okta, or any OIDC-compliant source, must configure federation manually through unsupported exception procedures and request support exceptions. This feature makes OpenShift the single identity broker for RHOSO: users authenticate through OpenShift (which already supports enterprise IdPs), and Keystone consumes those identities via federation. One identity plane, one configuration surface, zero duplicate IdP integrations.

A completed spike (OSPRH-27722, closed April 2026) proved the full brokered flow works end-to-end: Horizon login redirects to OpenShift, OpenShift delegates to an external IdP (Keycloak tested), and the user lands back in OpenStack with a properly scoped federated token. Authorization mapping (project/role restriction) was validated. Six open questions remain, primarily around OCP's evolving authentication architecture (direct external OIDC mode, OAuth server deprecation) and multi-IdP claim propagation.

This is Priority #2 on the RHOSO 19 planning list and a Beta Candidate for the October 28, 2026 Beta milestone. It directly unblocks EntraID support (RHOSSTRAT-949, Critical priority), which is the single most requested Keystone feature from field teams. Recommendation: invest at MVP/Tech Preview scope for RHOSO 19 Beta, with a clear GA path for RHOSO 20.

----

h2. 2. Problem Statement

h3. The identity fragmentation problem

When Red Hat moved from OSP 17.1 (TripleO) to RHOSO 18.0 (operator-based on OpenShift), the supported identity integration surface shrank. OSP 17.1 supported LDAP, ADFS, Red Hat SSO (Keycloak), and IdM out of the box with documented configuration paths. RHOSO 18.0 technically supports OIDC federation, but the configuration requires injecting Apache {{mod_auth_openidc}} overrides via Kubernetes Secrets ({{keystone-httpd-override}}), managing redirect URIs manually, and navigating undocumented edge cases. There is no Single Logout support. Non-Keycloak IdPs (EntraID, ADFS, Okta) require a support exception.

This creates three concrete problems:

# *Regression from OSP 17.1:* Customers migrating from OSP 17.1 lose identity integrations they had in production. The MAS customer escalated this directly to leadership. Troy Adianto Kartawinata (SA) stated: "I would much prefer that we don't do trial and error in customer environment as it will further impacting negatively the customer perception on our product maturity."
# *Duplicate identity configuration:* RHOSO runs on OpenShift. OpenShift already has a mature identity layer supporting Keycloak, EntraID, LDAP, OIDC, and SAML. Today, customers must configure identity twice -- once for OCP, once for Keystone -- with no connection between the two. This is operationally wasteful and a source of configuration drift.
# *EntraID blockage:* EntraID/Azure AD support (RHOSSTRAT-949, Critical priority, RHOSRFE-166 with telco label, request from Comcast) is blocked because we cannot test and certify non-Keycloak IdPs against the current manual federation path. The Keystone-OCP integration solves this structurally: any IdP that OpenShift supports becomes automatically available to Keystone.

h3. User story

{quote}As an OpenStack administrator, I want to authenticate my users in OpenShift and use them in OpenStack, so that I maintain a single identity plane across my hybrid infrastructure.{quote}

_(Source: OSPRH-27722 spike description and FR5/FR6 planning document)_

----

h2. 3. Customer Evidence

||Customer / Account||Signal Type||Detail||Source||
|*MAS (Malaysia)*|Escalation|Multiple AD domain integration with Horizon login is "mandatory." Escalated to Ashesh (leadership). LDAP backend works via CLI but Horizon always authenticates against local Keystone.|RHOSSTRAT-949 comments (Riyandi Himawan, Gil Rosenberg, Troy Kartawinata)|
|*Comcast*|RFE|Requested EntraID OIDC support for Keystone. Explicitly asked for both Horizon and CLI authentication paths.|RHOSRFE-166 (JP filed, David Waiting commented)|
|*Telefonica*|Multi-region|Single Keystone, Multiple OpenStacks (SKMO) pattern for multi-region. Used WebSSO with OIDC federation in testing. Directly exercises the federation machinery this feature improves.|RHOSSTRAT-949 comments (Owen McGonagle's Telefonica config), FR5/FR6 planning doc|
|*KDDI*|Architecture|"Shift on Stack" with Global Region pattern, single Keystone across all regions. Requires robust federated identity.|OCPSTRAT-2944|
|*Vietnam MoPS*|Architecture|SKMO pattern. Same unified identity requirement as KDDI.|FR5/FR6 planning doc|
|*Core42*|Federation|Keycloak federation options explored. Customer presentation on federation architecture.|Google Doc (Core42 Keycloak Federation Options)|
|*General field*|Support exception|Any customer using a non-Keycloak IdP with RHOSO 18.0 currently requires a support exception document. The OKTA exception document (April 2026) details the manual complexity.|OKTA Support Exception doc|

*Assessment:* Customer evidence is strong. Confidence: *High*. This is not speculative demand, it is a regression from a capability customers had in OSP 17.1, compounded by the structural opportunity of unifying identity through OCP.

----

h2. 4. Current State (RHOSO 18.0 FR6)

h3. What works today

* *OIDC federation with Keycloak:* Supported, but requires manual configuration of {{mod_auth_openidc}} via a Kubernetes Secret injected into the Keystone pod. The operator does not expose federation parameters natively.
* *LDAP backend:* Functional for CLI authentication. Horizon login against LDAP domains requires manual {{customServiceConfig}} overrides for multi-domain support ({{OPENSTACK_KEYSTONE_MULTIDOMAIN_SUPPORT}}, {{OPENSTACK_KEYSTONE_DOMAIN_DROPDOWN}}, {{OPENSTACK_KEYSTONE_DOMAIN_CHOICES}}).
* *WebSSO for Horizon:* Configurable through {{customServiceConfig}} but not operator-managed. Tested in Telefonica multi-region environment.

h3. What does not work or is unsupported

* *Non-Keycloak OIDC IdPs (EntraID, ADFS, Okta):* Configuration is known but untested and unsupported. Requires support exception.
* *Single Logout:* Not supported in RHOSO 18.0 federation.
* *Operator-managed federation:* The keystone-operator does not expose federation configuration. All federation setup is manual Kubernetes Secret injection.
* *Unified OCP-OpenStack identity:* No connection between OCP's identity layer and Keystone. Two separate identity planes.

h3. Spike results (OSPRH-27722, Closed)

The spike, led by Grzegorz Grasza (initial prototype) and Veronika Fisarova (validation and extension), ran from March-May 2026 and produced definitive results:

*Confirmed working:*

||Capability||Status||Detail||
|Service account identity flow|Supported|Existing Keystone federation works with K8s/OCP service account JWTs. No new code needed.|
|Human user browser login (OCP OAuth)|Supported|Requires Greg's new {{k8s_token}} middleware (prototype on Gerrit). Opaque OCP OAuth tokens handled.|
|Full brokered flow (Horizon -> OCP -> Keycloak -> OCP -> OpenStack)|Confirmed|Tested with user "Alice" created only in Keycloak. No additional OpenStack-side config needed.|
|Authorization mapping / restriction|Confirmed|User "Bob" mapped to limited project/group. Could not access admin project. Alice retained full access. Keystone federation mapping works correctly.|
|Federated token correctness|Confirmed|Token contains {{methods: ["k8s_token"]}}, {{OS-FEDERATION.identity_provider = k8s}}, {{OS-FEDERATION.protocol = k8s_token}}.|

*Not yet validated (open questions from spike, per Veronika's May 6 update):*

# {{k8s_token}} / TokenReview behavior with OCP direct external OIDC mode (newer OCP auth path)
# Whether to use direct TokenReview vs. {{kube-rbac-proxy}} (OCP's recommended layered-operator pattern)
# Group/claim propagation across external IdPs beyond Keycloak
# OpenStack-only user restrictions in OpenShift (users who authenticate through OCP but should not access OCP itself)
# Separation of service account / workload identity scope from human-user SSO scope
# Performance/latency impact of the brokered flow

----

h2. 5. Proposed Solution

h3. Architecture: OCP as identity broker

The solution uses OpenShift as the identity broker for RHOSO. This is explicitly *not* Keystone-NG (the Rust-based upstream rewrite tracked in RHOSSTRAT-1223). The team evaluated and decided: keep regular Keystone, use OCP as the user source. This is the right call, it leverages OCP's existing, mature, tested identity infrastructure rather than betting on an unproven upstream rewrite. the solution has to work for both CLI and Horizon access.

*Authentication flow:*

{noformat}User -> Horizon/CLI -> OpenShift OAuth/OIDC -> [External IdP] -> OpenShift -> Keystone (k8s_token federation) -> OpenStack token{noformat}

*Key design elements:*

# *New Keystone middleware (*{{k8s_token}}*):* Greg Grasza's prototype handles opaque OCP OAuth tokens and browser WebSSO flow. This is the primary new code artifact.
# *Keystone federation mapping:* Standard Keystone federation machinery maps OCP-brokered identities to OpenStack projects, groups, and roles. Already validated in the spike.
# *Operator integration (keystone-operator):* The operator must expose federation configuration parameters so that the manual Secret injection is no longer required. This is the productization gap.
# *Horizon WebSSO configuration:* Operator-managed WebSSO settings to enable the browser login redirect flow.

h3. MVP scope (RHOSSTRAT-1343)

Based on the spike findings and open questions, the MVP should demonstrate:

* End-to-end browser login: Horizon -> OCP -> External IdP -> OCP -> OpenStack
* CLI authentication via OCP token
* Authorization mapping (project/role scoping for federated users)
* At least two IdP backends validated: Keycloak (done) + EntraID (critical gap)
* Operator-managed federation configuration (no manual Secret injection)

h3. What MVP explicitly excludes

* Full multi-IdP certification matrix (defer to GA)
* Performance optimization of the brokered flow
* Single Logout support
* {{kube-rbac-proxy}} integration (needs architecture decision first)

----

h2. 6. Technical Considerations

h3. OCP authentication architecture evolution

This is the highest technical risk. OpenShift is deprecating its built-in OAuth server in favor of direct external OIDC mode (OCP 4.21+ documentation references this). The spike tested against the existing OAuth path. Veronika's May 6 update explicitly flags:

{quote}"We still need to confirm what changes when OpenShift is configured in the newer direct external OIDC mode, especially: whether TokenReview still returns stable user/groups for human users, whether the current Keystone mapping still works, whether the WebSSO part depends on the built-in OAuth /authorize flow and needs redesign."{quote}

*Implication:* The spike's proven flow may need rework if OCP moves to direct external OIDC as the primary path. This must be validated before committing to a GA timeline.

h3. TokenReview vs. kube-rbac-proxy

OCP's security team recommended investigating {{kube-rbac-proxy}} as the supported layered-operator pattern (per the May 6 discussion notes). The question is whether {{kube-rbac-proxy}} provides enough identity information for Keystone federation mapping, or whether direct TokenReview remains necessary.

*Recommendation:* Pursue both in parallel during MVP. If {{kube-rbac-proxy}} provides sufficient claims, prefer it for supportability. If not, document why direct TokenReview is required and get OCP team sign-off.

h3. OpenStack-only user isolation

The spike revealed that Keycloak users could log into the OpenShift web console and retrieve CLI login commands -- meaning an "OpenStack-only" user gets unintended OCP platform access. Veronika's suggested approach:

* External IdP group {{openstack-users}}
* OpenShift allows the login flow but RBAC denies console/API usage for that group

This is architecturally sound but needs validation and documentation as a supported pattern.

h3. Cross-team dependency

This feature requires coordination between the Keystone/Identity team (Veronika F., Grzegorz G.) and the OCP Authentication team. The May 6 discussion with the OCP security manager already happened. References shared include Dex documentation (GitOps operator pattern) and {{kube-rbac-proxy}}.

----

h2. 7. Competitive Landscape

*Evidence quality: Low.* I did not find direct competitive intelligence in the searched sources. The following is based on general market knowledge and should be verified.

* *VMware/Broadcom vSphere:* Tight vCenter-AD integration is table stakes. Customers migrating from VMware expect equivalent identity integration maturity.
* *Canonical OpenStack (Charmed):* Supports Keystone federation with OIDC and SAML. Does not have an equivalent "use the orchestration platform as identity broker" story because Canonical's orchestration layer (Juju/MAAS) is not an identity platform.
* *AWS/Azure/GCP:* Native IAM with federated identity is deeply integrated. This is the bar enterprise customers measure against, even for on-prem.

*The competitive argument is not "catch up to a specific competitor" but "close the regression from OSP 17.1 and deliver the unified identity story that OCP-based deployment uniquely enables."* No competitor has the structural advantage of an enterprise Kubernetes platform (OCP) as the deployment substrate for OpenStack. This feature turns that structural advantage into a user-facing benefit.

----

h2. 8. Success Criteria

h3. MVP (RHOSO 19 Tech Preview)

||Criterion||Measurement||Owner||
|End-to-end browser login works with Keycloak behind OCP|Demo in staging environment|Veronika F. / Grzegorz G.|
|End-to-end browser login works with EntraID behind OCP|Demo in staging environment|Engineering (needs assignment)|
|CLI authentication via OCP-brokered token|Functional test|Engineering|
|Authorization mapping restricts federated users correctly|Repeat Alice/Bob test from spike with operator-managed config|Engineering|
|Federation config is operator-managed (no manual Secret injection)|keystone-operator CR exposes federation parameters|Engineering|
|OpenStack-only user isolation documented|Architecture decision document + runbook|PM + Engineering|

h3. GA (RHOSO 20, planned)

||Criterion||Measurement||
|IdP certification matrix: Keycloak, EntraID, ADFS, Okta|QE test results for each|
|Performance impact quantified (<200ms added latency for auth flow)|Load test results|
|OCP direct external OIDC mode validated|QE test results|
|Single Logout support|Functional test|
|Customer adoption: 2+ customers in production|Field reports|

----

h2. 9. Risks and Open Questions

h3. Risks

||Risk||Severity||Likelihood||Mitigation||
|OCP OAuth deprecation breaks the proven spike flow|High|Medium|Validate against OCP direct external OIDC mode immediately (this is the #1 engineering priority for this feature)|
|EntraID testing reveals claim/group propagation issues|Medium|Medium|Start EntraID testing early; involve David Waiting (Comcast SA who requested it) for validation|
|RHOSO 19 Beta timeline (Oct 28) is too tight for MVP quality|Medium|Medium|Scope MVP ruthlessly; defer {{kube-rbac-proxy}} decision and multi-IdP matrix to GA|
|OCP team does not endorse direct TokenReview long-term|Medium|Low|The May 6 discussion happened; maintain that relationship. {{kube-rbac-proxy}}is the fallback.|

h3. Open questions requiring answers before Beta

# *Does the* {{k8s_token}} *middleware work with OCP direct external OIDC mode?* (Assigned: Grzegorz G., per Veronika's May 6 update)
# *TokenReview vs.* {{kube-rbac-proxy}}*:* Which approach for Keystone? Architecture decision needed by end of July 2026.
# *OpenStack-only user isolation:* Is the "IdP group + OCP RBAC deny" pattern supportable? OCP team sign-off needed.
# *RHOSSTRAT-1343 description:* The Initiative ticket is empty ("Creating code for demonstrational purposes"). Needs proper description, acceptance criteria, and MVP scope definition. _This is what JP was tagged to do on July 8._

----

h2. 10. Recommendation

*Confidence: High*

Invest in Keystone-OCP integration at MVP / Tech Preview scope for RHOSO 19 Beta (October 28, 2026), with a defined path to GA in RHOSO 19.

*Rationale:*

# *The spike proved feasibility.* This is not speculative engineering. The full brokered flow works. Authorization mapping works. The remaining questions are about OCP platform evolution and productization, not "can this be done."
# *It structurally solves the EntraID problem.* Instead of testing and certifying every IdP against Keystone's {{mod_auth_openidc}}path individually, this feature makes OCP the certification surface. Any IdP that works with OCP works with RHOSO. This is architecturally elegant and operationally efficient.
# *Customer demand is real and escalated.* MAS, Comcast, and Telefonica are not hypothetical. The identity regression from OSP 17.1 is actively damaging product perception.
# *The window is right.* Engineering has momentum from the spike. The lead engineers (Veronika F., Grzegorz G.) are engaged and have produced detailed findings. Delaying loses this momentum.

*What would change this recommendation:*

* If validation against OCP direct external OIDC mode fails fundamentally (not "needs tweaks" but "the architecture doesn't work"), descope to an engineering spike for RHOSO 19 and defer MVP to RHOSO 20.
* If the OCP team signals that TokenReview for human users will be unsupported in OCP 4.next, the timeline needs reassessment.

----

[SRIOV Metrics for RCA and Capacity Planning|https://docs.google.com/document/d/124cj2RYanhSm94P-LXYYMZ7xadmrIDB4Mn9OT3gEZFg/edit?usp=sharing]

To support the Unified Observability next-generation initiative, statistics and events need to be exposed for SRIOV setups to OpenShift Observability, which is based on prometheus for data collection, so this be also done as part of openstack-network-exporter.

 

The focus of this feature is to implement a  Prometheus exporter for SRIOV and integrate it with RHOSO. Metrics collection for each of the individual metrics categories and metrics identification are defined in separate epics.

 

From Operator side we have [https://github.com/openshift/sriov-network-metrics-exporter|https://github.com/openshift/sriov-network-metrics-exporter] , As part of this Ticket we have to explore any SRIOV metrics we have to collect/expose from the dataplane nodes

 

*Acceptance criteria:*

1) Provide prometheus export of SR-IOV metrics relevant for RCA and capacity planning 

*Definition of Done:*
1) Document all the supported/exported metrics (FR6 targeted for Tech Preview, we can skip the official documentation, GA will be FR7)
2) Add metrics validations in CI and all metrics check should pass

*Summary*:  TOBE refined - and added to a new storage outcome for quality coverage improvements



*Background:*

Run the upstream functional tests which requires a full deployment (not a mocked one) for python-<foo>client repositories.

Right now we don't have coverage in CI for repositories like python-<foo>client. Several of these repositories provides a set of functional tests. Those tests are meant to be executed against a real deployment, not a mocked one. In the upstream gates ([http://opendev.org|http://opendev.org|smart-link] ) are executed against devstack, but they can really be executed also against any deployed OpenStack.

[https://codesearch.opendev.org/?q=parent%3A%20devstack-tox-functional&i=nope&literal=nope&files=&excludeFiles=&repos=|https://codesearch.opendev.org/?q=parent%3A%20devstack-tox-functional&i=nope&literal=nope&files=&excludeFiles=&repos=|smart-link] 

This is especially useful for testing clients (OSC), which we don't have basically any  testing now.

As we are missing testing, this epic is about running such tests from the source code that we ship.

DoD:

component jobs for the appropriate component which runs the functional tests in

* python-cinderclient
* glance_store
* python-glanceclient
* python-manilaclient
* python-swiftclient

This requires the creation of an abstract job that can be inherited in zuul.

items.fromString:
*Summary*

Customers are in need to be able to change the current glance image storage backend to a different one, such as from CEPH to S3. This should be possible for existing installations where changing backends is currently not supported by Red Hat.

* Change the current CEPH backend to S3 for an existing installation.
* A clear way to migrate the images is present and documented.
* Impact on existing workload is minimal.

*Why does the customer need this?*

Customer is using CEPH only as a Glance image backend and would like to consolidate/move away from CEPH for it.

h4. *Additional Information:*

From discussions about this issue, the following high-level steps where discussed:

* Enabling multistore to mirror images
* Enable copy_image import method
* Copy image from CEPH to S3 which will keep same image id and properties
* Delete image from CEPH
* Remove CEPH backend from configuration
* To actually copy image a command as follows could be possible:
** glance image-import --import-method copy-image --stores store1,store2 image-id

*Next:*

* add Epics for doc, validation, support enablement if needed (docs likey cover it)

Currently, Horizon interacts with Nova using python-novaclient. The OpenStack community is moving toward openstacksdk as the primary library, leaving individual service clients in a "maintenance-only" state for some features. The goal is to replace openstack_dashboard.api.nova calls with the openstack.compute proxy provided by the SDK.

 We need to implement the openstacksdk compute proxy and start replacing api.nova calls resource by resource. We will start with Flavors in this task.

items.fromString: Update RHOSO-18 Ceph client libraries to ceph9 for longer term support
items.toString: Update RHOSO-18 Ceph client libraries to ceph9

items.fromString:
*Initiative Overview* 

RHOSO-18 had to ship with Ceph7 clients at GA and original Ceph supported release was Ceph8.  We are now supporting Ceph9 and we need to consider the mismatched RHOSO/Ceph lifecycles.

Before we reach RHCS 7 ELS, we need to update the RHOSO-18 client libraries to ceph9 for longer terms support and to get critical bug fixes and CVEs.

In addtion with the need to maintain +/-2 version client compatibility, we need to have a newer client version in RHOSO-18 as we look ahead to 18->19 upgrades with Ceph10.



*Goals:*

# Pre-test ceph9 clients with RHOSO-18
# Update RHOSO-18 to replace ceph7 client libs with ceph9 (Reldel)
# Document procedure for brownfield customers to update
# Ensure no regressions to RHOSO CI tests with ceph9 clients 

*Done - Acceptance Criteria* 
1. RHOSO-18 ships with Ceph9.1 client libs

*Out of Scope* 

* RHOSO-18 only - so nothing here is for older releases or RHOSO-19, though it also helps with the upgrade path there



*Documentation Impact:*  

None

*Release Delivery Impact;*

Yes

We need to rebuild using the ceph 9 client libs

h2. Summary

[https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3304|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3304|smart-link]  is an OpenShift on OpenStack feature to enable OpenShift clusters installed on Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift (RHOSO) via IPI to consume block storage from Cinder when Cinder brokers Dell PowerFlex using native ScaleIO protocols. Today, tenants cannot use performant PowerFlex-backed volumes through Cinder-CSI on bare-metal / Shift-on-Stack worker nodes. 

That OCP feature tracks productization and delivery of the plumbing required for Cinder-CSI to provision, attach, and mount PowerFlex volumes brokered by Cinder.

This Initiative tracks the OpenStack cinder work needed to provide the logic needed to attach and detach cinder volumes from the OCP Cinder CSI driver.

*Team direction:* Delivery is expected to leverage *os-brick* functionality on bare-metal worker nodes — running os-brick in a sidecar container alongside Cinder-CSI to handle ScaleIO (and other protocol) attach/detach operations that cannot be performed by the standard VM-oriented CSI node plugin path.

*Source RFE:* [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOSRFE-205|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOSRFE-205|smart-link]  

*Feature Details:* [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3304|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3304|smart-link] 

----

h2. Goals 

* Implement bare-metal volume attachment using *os-brick* (sidecar-based connector model) as the chosen architectural approach.
* Enable the ability for Cinder-CSI can authenticate to Cinder/PowerFlex using the RBAC/Token model.
* Enable the support standard volume lifecycle operations (create, attach, stage, publish, mount, delete) for PowerFlex-backed volumes on bare-metal workers.
* Coordinate delivery across Shift-on-Stack (bare-metal plumbing) and Storage/Cinder (PowerFlex driver behavior).
* Provide input to OCP feature documentation as needed

h2. Acceptance Criteria 

* Resulting Cinder functionality provided to OCP feature supports:
** OpenShift cluster on RHOSO can provision and mount a PVC backed by a PowerFlex Cinder volume on a bare-metal worker using Cinder-CSI.
** Bare-metal volume attach/detach is performed via *os-brick* sidecar integration (not the standard VM-only node path).
** Cinder-CSI uses RBAC/Token authentication successfully against the PowerFlex-backed Cinder endpoint.
** Standard volume operations (create, attach, mount, delete) succeed without manual operator intervention beyond documented configuration
* PowerFlex client/kernel prerequisites on bare-metal nodes and os-brick sidecar requirements are documented and validated.
* Known limitations are documented.

h2. Open Questions:

items.fromString:
h2. Feature Overview (mandatory — complete while in New status)

Enable OpenShift clusters installed on Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift (RHOSO) via IPI to consume block storage from Cinder when Cinder brokers Dell PowerFlex using native ScaleIO protocols.

Today, tenants cannot reliably use performant PowerFlex-backed volumes through Cinder-CSI on bare-metal / Shift-on-Stack worker nodes. This feature tracks productization and delivery of the plumbing required for Cinder-CSI to provision, attach, and mount PowerFlex volumes brokered by Cinder.

*Source RFE:* RHOSRFE-205

*Team direction:* Delivery is expected to leverage *os-brick* functionality on bare-metal worker nodes — running os-brick in a sidecar container alongside Cinder-CSI to handle ScaleIO (and other protocol) attach/detach operations that cannot be performed by the standard VM-oriented CSI node plugin path.

----

h2. Goals (mandatory — complete while in New status)

* Allow OpenShift on RHOSO (IPI) to consume PowerFlex-backed Cinder volumes via Cinder-CSI using ScaleIO-native attachment where supported.
* Implement bare-metal volume attachment using *os-brick* (sidecar-based connector model) as the chosen architectural approach.
* Ensure Cinder-CSI can authenticate to Cinder/PowerFlex using the RBAC/Token model.
* Support standard volume lifecycle operations (create, attach, stage, publish, mount, delete) for PowerFlex-backed volumes on bare-metal workers.
* Coordinate delivery across Shift-on-Stack (bare-metal plumbing) and Storage/Cinder (PowerFlex driver behavior).

*Who benefits:* Customers using Dell PowerFlex as their block platform who deploy OpenShift on RHOSO and need tenant PVCs backed by performant native protocols.

*Difference from today:* PowerFlex volumes may be available in Cinder for VMs, but bare-metal OpenShift workers lack the kernel module, client binaries, and Cinder-CSI attachment path needed for ScaleIO protocol consumption.

----

h2. Requirements (mandatory — complete while in Refinement status)

||Requirement||Notes||isMVP?||
|Bare-metal / CoreOS nodes (IPI or OpenShift MachineSet on RHOSO) can use Dell PowerFlex ScaleIO kernel module and volume client components as required|Depends on Shift-on-Stack / SOS delivery|Yes|
|Cinder-CSI on bare-metal nodes uses *os-brick* (sidecar connector) for volume attach/detach operations|Chosen team direction; includes ScaleIO SDC client and kernel module support in the sidecar|Yes|
|Cinder-CSI communicates with PowerFlex brokered by Cinder using RBAC/Token authentication|Align with current Cinder auth model|Yes|
|Cinder-CSI performs standard volume operations (provision, attach, stage, publish, mount, expand, delete) with PowerFlex/Cinder backends|Include error handling and teardown|Yes|
|Cinder-CSI can connect/mount volumes from Cinder using ScaleIO protocol on supported worker nodes|Via os-brick connector on BM nodes|Yes|
|Documented deployment and configuration requirements for operators|Include PowerFlex-specific parameters, os-brick sidecar prerequisites, and node requirements|Yes|
|Validation on representative RHOSO + OCP version combination|Coordinate with QE / spike outcomes|Yes|

----

h2. Done — Acceptance Criteria (mandatory — complete while in Refinement status)

* [ ] OpenShift cluster on RHOSO can provision and mount a PVC backed by a PowerFlex Cinder volume on a bare-metal worker using Cinder-CSI.
* [ ] Bare-metal volume attach/detach is performed via *os-brick* sidecar integration (not the standard VM-only node path).
* [ ] Cinder-CSI uses RBAC/Token authentication successfully against the PowerFlex-backed Cinder endpoint.
* [ ] Standard volume operations (create, attach, mount, delete) succeed without manual operator intervention beyond documented configuration.
* [ ] ScaleIO client/kernel prerequisites on bare-metal nodes and os-brick sidecar requirements are documented and validated.
* [ ] Feature is linked to RHOSRFE-205 and downstream epics/stories are traceable from this Feature.
* [ ] Known limitations are documented.

----

h2. Use Cases — User Experience & Workflow (Refinement)

# *Platform admin* deploys RHOSO with Shift-on-Stack bare-metal workers and enables Cinder-CSI with PowerFlex backend configuration and os-brick sidecar on node pods.
# *Tenant* creates a PVC; Cinder provisions a PowerFlex volume; Cinder-CSI controller publishes connection info; the node plugin delegates attach to os-brick, which performs ScaleIO map/connect; the volume is staged and mounted on the bare-metal worker.
# *Platform admin* upgrades or scales MachineSets; os-brick-based attachment behavior remains consistent across nodes meeting prerequisites.

----

h2. Documentation Considerations (Refinement)

* Operator guide: PowerFlex + Cinder-CSI prerequisites on bare-metal (kernel module, SDC/client, network).
* os-brick sidecar deployment model: container image contents, privileged access, host namespace requirements.
* Integration with RHOSO / Shift-on-Stack deployment documentation.
* Troubleshooting guide for common attach/mount failures.

----

h2. Background and Strategic Fit (Refinement)

*Business justification (from RHOSRFE-205):* Dell PowerFlex is the block storage customers use; tenants need to consume it via performant native protocols (ScaleIO) on OpenShift deployed on RHOSO.

*Architectural direction:* Prototype work (OSASINFRA-4334) validated an os-brick sidecar approach — a privileged container running os-brick with ScaleIO SDC client binaries and kernel module support, exposing a gRPC connector interface to the Cinder-CSI node plugin. This is the intended delivery path for bare-metal volume attachment.

*Contacts (from RFE):*

* Greg Procunier (gprocuni@redhat.com)
* Andrew Austin (aaustin@redhat.com)

items.fromString:
## Initiative Overview

Develop training material for GSS (Global Support Services) to enable effective support of chargeback functionality in Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift. This initiative covers the creation and delivery of documentation and training content that equips GSS engineers to debug, troubleshoot, and validate chargeback enablement, including storage domain connectivity, Operator configuration, and telemetry data collection.

## Goals

- Provide GSS with training material that enables them to independently troubleshoot and resolve common chargeback support cases
- Ensure GSS engineers understand the end-to-end chargeback data flow from telemetry collection through storage and reporting
- Reduce escalations to engineering by equipping GSS with the knowledge to diagnose standard enablement and operational issues

## Acceptance Criteria

- Training material is created, reviewed, and made available to GSS
- Material covers how to validate chargeback has been enabled along with storage domain connections
- Material covers standard enablement issues as a cloud administrator including storage domain issues and Operator enablement
- Material covers how to determine that chargeback has been enabled and is operating nominally
- Material covers how to validate telemetry data is being collected and stored properly
- GSS team has been consulted on specific areas they would like covered

## Out of Scope

- Development of new chargeback features or functionality
- Automated tooling for chargeback diagnostics
- Customer-facing documentation (this initiative targets internal GSS enablement only)

*Feature Request Overview (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_{_}
{_}{{_}}What user goal or problem do you need to solve?{_} 

When using DCN or DZ the image import process is sequential i.e one store at a time. For use cases where large images are imported into multiple stores this can significantly impact the time it takes for the image to become available across the environment.

This RFE aims at parallelising the import process so that images can be imported in multiple stores at the same time.

*Business justification (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
_How would this feature benefit the customer?_

Reduce the time it takes to import images to DZ or DCN environments (multi stores) so that users can faster consume the aforementioned images.

*Functional requirements (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_{_}
{_}{{_}}What do you want the result of this feature to be? Add as many requirements as needed.{_}

* Parallelise the image import process
* Expose an option to set the number of parallel imports.

*Describe the customer impact*

IMPORTANT: Do not include customer names.

* Provide links to the account project
* Provide links to any related support tickets (open or closed)

For details on connecting Jira issues to an account, see [Connecting Jira Issues to Accounts|https://redhat.atlassian.net/wiki/pages/viewpage.action?spaceKey=JiraAid&title=Tracking+Customer+and+Partner+Requests+in+Red+Hat+Jira#TrackingCustomerandPartnerRequestsinRedHatJira-ConnectingJiraIssuestoAccounts].

 

*Feature Request Overview (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_{_}
{_}_What user goal or problem do you need to solve?_ 
Current image_size_total behavior accepts any size of image while the total size is exceeded.
This means that the quota only works for the situation that the image size total is already exceeded.
For example, image_size_total sets 10 MiB. The current behavior accepts an image whose size is larger than 10MiB.
This is not an ideal quota behavior because quota should work as the limit to the size.

The ideal behavior is as follows if image_size_total sets to 10MiB.

# Image can be uploaded until the total size including all uploaded image is equal or less than image_size_total.
# If the total size is less than image_size_total, the only accepted image size is (image_size_total - the total size of the current images).


 

*Business justification (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
_How would this feature benefit the customer?_
The current import method for multi stores is sequential which heavily impact the time it takes to import images to multiple zones or sites. This means images can take time to be available for the workloads to boot from.
This feature aims at parallelising the import process so that images can be imported in multiple stores at the same time.

*Functional requirements (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_{_}
{_}_What do you want the result of this feature to be? Add as many requirements as needed._

* Add parallelism into the import workflow when using multistores
* Default remains serial (no change)
* Modular: Admin can set the number of store imported in parallel.

*Describe the customer impact*

* When using DZ or DCN, imports can be serialised reducing the time it takes for an image to be available.
* VMs can be started faster.

Spec
[https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/glance-specs/+/967046|https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/glance-specs/+/967046]

Implement a max_parallel_stores option to define how many stores can be imported in parallel (default is 1),  it uses a work queue and a worker pool.

*Functional requirements (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_{_}
{_}{{_}}What do you want the result of this feature to be? Add as many requirements as needed.{_}

* Parallelise the image import process
* Expose an option to set the number of parallel imports.

*Describe the customer impact*

IMPORTANT: Do not include customer names.

* Provide links to the account project
* Provide links to any related support tickets (open or closed)

For details on connecting Jira issues to an account, see [Connecting Jira Issues to Accounts|https://redhat.atlassian.net/wiki/pages/viewpage.action?spaceKey=JiraAid&title=Tracking+Customer+and+Partner+Requests+in+Red+Hat+Jira#TrackingCustomerandPartnerRequestsinRedHatJira-ConnectingJiraIssuestoAccounts].

 

*Feature Request Overview (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_{_}
{_}_What user goal or problem do you need to solve?_ 
Current image_size_total behavior accepts any size of image while the total size is exceeded.
This means that the quota only works for the situation that the image size total is already exceeded.
For example, image_size_total sets 10 MiB. The current behavior accepts an image whose size is larger than 10MiB.
This is not an ideal quota behavior because quota should work as the limit to the size.

The ideal behavior is as follows if image_size_total sets to 10MiB.

# Image can be uploaded until the total size including all uploaded image is equal or less than image_size_total.
# If the total size is less than image_size_total, the only accepted image size is (image_size_total - the total size of the current images).


 

*Business justification (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
_How would this feature benefit the customer?_
The current import method for multi stores is sequential which heavily impact the time it takes to import images to multiple zones or sites. This means images can take time to be available for the workloads to boot from.
This feature aims at parallelising the import process so that images can be imported in multiple stores at the same time.

*Functional requirements (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_{_}
{_}_What do you want the result of this feature to be? Add as many requirements as needed._

* Add parallelism into the import workflow when using multistores
* Default remains serial (no change)
* Modular: Admin can set the number of store imported in parallel.

*Describe the customer impact*

* When using DZ or DCN, imports can be serialised reducing the time it takes for an image to be available.
* VMs can be started faster.

Spec
[https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/glance-specs/+/967046|https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/glance-specs/+/967046]

Implement a max_parallel_stores option to define how many stores can be imported in parallel (default is 1),  it uses a work queue and a worker pool.
