items.toString:
h2. 1. Executive Summary

OpenStack Resource Controller (ORC) is a Kubernetes operator that enables declarative, GitOps-style management of OpenStack infrastructure resources via Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). This PRD defines the requirements for the initial productization of ORC as a Tech Preview offering within the Red Hat OpenStack portfolio, exposing Kubernetes-native lifecycle management of OpenStack networking, compute, and image resources to platform engineering teams and OpenShift-on-OpenStack operators. The Tech Preview release will establish the foundation for a supported, production-quality operator while clearly communicating the maturity boundaries of individual controllers.

----

h2. 2. Problem Statement

h3. 2.1 Current State

Managing OpenStack infrastructure resources today requires direct interaction with the OpenStack API through imperative tooling (OpenStack CLI, Heat templates, Terraform), which creates challenges for teams that operate in Kubernetes-centric or GitOps-oriented environments. There is no native, Kubernetes-idiomatic way to declare, reconcile, or audit OpenStack resources alongside Kubernetes workloads. The upstream ORC project (github.com/k-orc/openstack-resource-controller) provides a functional Kubernetes operator for this purpose but has not yet been productized, packaged, or supported as a Red Hat offering.

h3. 2.2 Desired State

ORC is available as an officially released Tech Preview product from Red Hat, installable on OpenShift clusters. Platform teams can declaratively manage a defined set of OpenStack resources using Kubernetes manifests, benefit from continuous reconciliation and drift detection, and integrate ORC into GitOps pipelines. The release clearly delineates which controllers are Tech-Preview-supported, which are experimental, and what is out of scope for this release.

h3. 2.3 Business Impact

* Accelerates adoption of OpenShift on OpenStack by providing a Kubernetes-native control plane for the underlying OpenStack infrastructure.
* Reduces operational toil for platform teams managing OpenStack resources in conjunction with Kubernetes workloads.
* Positions Red Hat as the supported upstream steward of ORC, strengthening the CAPO (Cluster API Provider OpenStack) ecosystem.
* Creates a differentiating capability for Red Hat OpenStack Platform customers migrating to cloud-native operational models.

----

h2. 3. Goals & Objectives

h3. Primary Goals

* Package and release ORC as a Tech Preview product installable via the OpenShift OperatorHub / OLM.
* Formally define and communicate the set of OpenStack controllers included in the Tech Preview scope.
* Clearly document and surface which controllers are mature/stable versus those that are immature/experimental within the Tech Preview release.
* Ensure Tech Preview release meets Red Hat quality gates for documentation, supportability, and security.
* Enable customers to manage mature OpenStack resources declaratively via Kubernetes CRDs.

h3. Success Metrics

||Metric||Current||Target||Measurement Method||
|Controllers available at Tech Preview|0 (no product)|≥ 9 stable controllers shipped|Controller inventory in release notes|
|Experimental controllers clearly flagged|0|100% of immature controllers carry explicit alpha/experimental annotation|Release notes and API annotation audit|
|Operator installable via OLM|No|Yes|Installation test on supported OpenShift version|
|Documentation coverage|None|All Tech Preview controllers have user-facing docs|Docs review gate|
|CI pass rate|N/A|≥ 95% on supported OpenShift + OpenStack version matrix|CI dashboard|

----

h2. 4. User Personas

h3. Persona 1: OpenShift Platform Engineer ("Platform Engineer")

* *Role*: Platform/infrastructure engineer responsible for managing OpenShift clusters running on OpenStack.
* *Goals*: Manage OpenStack networking, compute, and image resources using the same GitOps tooling and Kubernetes manifests already used to manage cluster workloads; avoid context-switching to the OpenStack CLI or Heat.
* *Pain Points*: Forced to use imperative OpenStack tooling outside the Kubernetes control plane; no drift detection or continuous reconciliation for OpenStack resources; difficulty auditing infrastructure changes alongside application changes.
* *Usage Context*: Day-to-day cluster operations, initial cluster bootstrap, infrastructure change management via GitOps pipelines.

h3. Persona 2: CAPO Operator / Cluster API User

* *Role*: Engineer or SRE using Cluster API Provider OpenStack (CAPO) to lifecycle-manage Kubernetes clusters on OpenStack.
* *Goals*: Use ORC as the infrastructure provider layer for CAPO to ensure declarative management of the OpenStack resources underpinning Kubernetes node pools and cluster networking.
* *Pain Points*: CAPO lacks a standardized, Kubernetes-native way to manage the prerequisite OpenStack infrastructure (networks, subnets, security groups, images) that clusters depend on; direct OpenStack API use is fragile and not reconciled.
* *Usage Context*: Cluster provisioning workflows, pre-flight infrastructure setup, integration testing of multi-cluster environments.

----

h2. 5. Requirements

h3. 5.1 Functional Requirements

||ID||Requirement||Priority||Acceptance Criteria||
|FR-001|ORC must be installable on supported OpenShift versions via OLM (OperatorHub or catalog source).|MVP|Installation completes without errors on the target OpenShift version matrix; operator pod reaches Running state.|
|FR-002|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *Network* resources.|MVP|A user can create, update, and delete an OpenStack Network by applying a Kubernetes manifest; reconciliation loop enforces desired state.|
|FR-003|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *Subnet* resources.|MVP|A user can create, update, and delete an OpenStack Subnet by applying a Kubernetes manifest; reconciliation loop enforces desired state.|
|FR-004|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *Router* resources.|MVP|A user can create, update, and delete an OpenStack Router by applying a Kubernetes manifest; reconciliation loop enforces desired state.|
|FR-005|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *SecurityGroup* resources.|MVP|A user can create, update, and delete an OpenStack Security Group and its rules by applying a Kubernetes manifest; reconciliation loop enforces desired state.|
|FR-006|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *FloatingIP* resources.|MVP|A user can allocate and release an OpenStack Floating IP by applying a Kubernetes manifest; reconciliation loop enforces desired state.|
|FR-007|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *Port* resources.|MVP|A user can create, update, and delete an OpenStack Port by applying a Kubernetes manifest; reconciliation loop enforces desired state.|
|FR-008|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *Image* resources.|MVP|A user can declare an OpenStack Glance image (including source URL and properties) by applying a Kubernetes manifest; the controller uploads and manages the image lifecycle.|
|FR-009|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *Flavor* resources.|MVP|A user can declare an OpenStack Compute Flavor by applying a Kubernetes manifest; reconciliation loop enforces desired state.|
|FR-010|ORC must expose a CRD and controller for managing OpenStack *KeyPair* resources.|MVP|A user can declare an OpenStack Compute Key Pair by applying a Kubernetes manifest; reconciliation loop enforces desired state.|
|FR-011|ORC must expose CRDs for *Server* and *ServerGroup* resources and label them explicitly as experimental/alpha in both the API and product documentation.|MVP|Server and ServerGroup CRDs are present; API annotations and release notes clearly mark them as not production-ready for this Tech Preview release.|
|FR-012|ORC must support adoption ("import") of pre-existing OpenStack resources into Kubernetes management without re-creating them.|MVP|A user can apply a manifest referencing an existing OpenStack resource by external ID or name; the controller reconciles without destroying and re-creating the resource.|
|FR-013|ORC must perform continuous drift detection and reconciliation for all managed resources.|MVP|If an OpenStack resource is modified out-of-band, ORC detects the drift within its reconciliation period and restores desired state (or surfaces the drift via status conditions).|
|FR-014|ORC must surface resource status, conditions, and error information on the Kubernetes object's {{.status}} field.|MVP|After applying a manifest, {{.status.conditions}} reflect the current state (Ready, Error, Reconciling); error messages are human-readable.|
|FR-015|ORC must support credential configuration for connecting to an OpenStack cloud (clouds.yaml / application credentials).|MVP|The operator accepts an OpenStack credential reference (Secret); resources are managed against the configured OpenStack endpoint.|
|FR-016|The Tech Preview release must include user-facing documentation covering installation, supported controllers, and known limitations.|MVP|Documentation is published and covers all FR-002 through FR-015 controllers, plus explicit experimental status of FR-011.|
|FR-017|ORC must expose metrics suitable for monitoring operator health.|Non-MVP|Metrics endpoint is available; reconciliation counts and error rates are exposed in Prometheus-compatible format.|

h3. 5.2 Non-Functional Requirements

||ID||Requirement||Category||Target||
|NFR-001|ORC must not require elevated (cluster-admin) privileges beyond what is necessary for CRD installation and operator pod execution.|Security|Least-privilege RBAC roles defined and documented.|
|NFR-002|ORC container images must be based on Red Hat Universal Base Image (UBI) and pass Red Hat image certification scanning.|Security|Image passes Red Hat certification pipeline with no critical CVEs.|
|NFR-003|The operator must be compatible with the OpenShift versions defined in the Tech Preview support matrix.|Compatibility|Passes e2e tests on all versions in the declared support matrix.|
|NFR-004|Reconciliation loop latency for stable controllers must not degrade OpenStack API responsiveness beyond reasonable polling intervals.|Performance|Reconciliation poll interval configurable; default does not trigger OpenStack API rate limiting under normal cluster load.|
|NFR-005|All CRDs and controller binaries must be versioned and follow a documented upgrade path for future releases.|Maintainability|Version labels present on all CRDs; upgrade documentation exists for the GA pathway.|

----

h2. 6. User Stories

*US-001*: As a Platform Engineer, I want to declare OpenStack networks, subnets, and security groups as Kubernetes manifests so that I can manage them via GitOps alongside my cluster workloads. - *Acceptance Criteria*:   - Given a Kubernetes cluster with ORC installed, when I apply a Network manifest, then ORC creates the corresponding OpenStack Network and reflects its status in {{.status.conditions}}.   - Given a GitOps pipeline, when I commit a change to a Network manifest, then ORC reconciles the change against OpenStack without manual CLI intervention.

*US-002*: As a Platform Engineer, I want ORC to detect and remediate drift on managed OpenStack resources so that manual out-of-band changes do not create infrastructure inconsistencies. - *Acceptance Criteria*:   - Given a managed SecurityGroup that is modified directly in OpenStack, when the reconciliation loop runs, then ORC restores the declared desired state and surfaces the drift event in the resource's status.

*US-003*: As a CAPO Operator, I want to adopt existing OpenStack networks and images into ORC management without re-creating them so that I can bring brownfield infrastructure under declarative control. - *Acceptance Criteria*:   - Given an existing OpenStack Network identified by name or ID, when I apply a manifest with the adoption annotation, then ORC takes ownership of the resource without deleting and recreating it.

*US-004*: As a Platform Engineer, I want ORC to be installable via OpenShift OperatorHub so that I can discover, install, and upgrade the operator through standard OLM tooling. - *Acceptance Criteria*:   - Given access to OperatorHub on a supported OpenShift version, when I search for ORC, then I can install it without leaving the OpenShift console or using manual kubectl commands.

*US-005*: As a Platform Engineer, I want the product documentation to clearly identify which ORC controllers are stable and which are experimental so that I understand the supportability boundaries before adopting each controller in production workflows. - *Acceptance Criteria*:   - Given the Tech Preview release documentation, when I look up the Server or ServerGroup controller, then I see an explicit experimental/alpha designation with an explanation of known limitations.

----

h2. 7. Scope

h3. In Scope

* Packaging and release of ORC as an OLM-based operator for OpenShift (Tech Preview).
* The following stable OpenStack controllers: Network, Subnet, Router, SecurityGroup, FloatingIP, Port, Image, Flavor, KeyPair.
* The following experimental controllers (shipped but explicitly marked alpha/not production-ready): Server, ServerGroup.
* Brownfield adoption (import) of existing OpenStack resources.
* Continuous drift detection and reconciliation.
* Resource status and conditions reporting via Kubernetes {{.status}} fields.
* OpenStack credential management via Kubernetes Secrets.
* User-facing documentation: installation guide, controller reference, known limitations.
* Release notes that enumerate controller maturity levels.

h3. Out of Scope

* General Availability (GA) / full support designation (this release is Tech Preview only).
* Controllers for OpenStack services not yet implemented upstream: Cinder Volumes, Octavia Load Balancers, Designate DNS, Swift Object Storage, Manila Shared File Systems.
* A graphical UI or OpenShift Console plugin for ORC.
* Multi-cloud or multi-region OpenStack federation.
* Production-readiness of the Server and ServerGroup controllers (these are experimental in this release).
* Automated migration tooling from Heat or Terraform to ORC.

----

h2. 8. Assumptions & Constraints

h3. Assumptions

* The target OpenShift version(s) for Tech Preview support will be confirmed before the release gates are finalized.
* The upstream ORC project (k-orc/openstack-resource-controller) will remain open source and Red Hat will contribute productization changes back upstream.
* Customers deploying ORC Tech Preview understand and accept the reduced support obligations of a Tech Preview offering.
* OpenStack environments targeted by ORC are compatible with the upstream-supported OpenStack API versions used by the operator.
* CAPO integration is a key use case but detailed CAPO interoperability testing is not required for Tech Preview.

h3. Constraints

* This release is designated *Tech Preview* only; production workload support is not implied.
* All container images must pass Red Hat image certification (UBI-based, no critical CVEs).
* The operator must be distributed via OLM/OperatorHub to align with Red Hat's standard operator delivery mechanism.
* Upstream API is versioned at {{v1alpha1}}; the product must not misrepresent this as a stable API version.

h3. Dependencies

* Upstream ORC project (github.com/k-orc/openstack-resource-controller) for source code and CRD definitions.
* Red Hat OLM / OperatorHub infrastructure for distribution.
* Red Hat image build and certification pipeline (UBI, RHCC).
* OpenShift release and support matrix team for declaring the supported OpenShift version range.
* Red Hat documentation team for publication of user-facing docs.

----

h2. 9. Risks & Mitigations

||Risk||Likelihood||Impact||Mitigation||
|Upstream API instability ({{v1alpha1}}) causes breaking changes between Tech Preview and GA|Medium|High|Pin the product to a specific upstream commit/tag; engage as upstream contributors to stabilize the API before GA commitment; communicate API volatility clearly in Tech Preview documentation.|
|Server and ServerGroup controllers are promoted prematurely and customers treat them as production-ready|Medium|Medium|Apply explicit {{alpha}} annotations to CRDs; include prominent warnings in documentation and release notes; require opt-in flag or annotation to use experimental controllers.|
|OpenStack version compatibility gaps cause failures on customer environments|Medium|High|Define and publish a tested OpenStack version compatibility matrix as part of the Tech Preview release; include version checks in operator startup.|
|Low customer adoption of Tech Preview limits feedback before GA planning|Low|Medium|Engage key CAPO/OpenShift-on-OpenStack accounts directly as early adopters; establish a feedback channel (Jira, mailing list, or Slack) referenced in the product documentation.|

----

h2. 10. Controller Maturity Reference

The following table summarizes the current maturity status of ORC controllers as of the Tech Preview release basis, derived from the upstream project state.

||Controller||OpenStack Service||Tech Preview Status||Notes||
|Network|Neutron|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|Subnet|Neutron|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|Router|Neutron|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|SecurityGroup|Neutron|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|FloatingIP|Neutron|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|Port|Neutron|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|Image|Glance|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|Flavor|Nova|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|KeyPair|Nova|*Stable*|Included in Tech Preview; recommended for production use within TP constraints.|
|Server|Nova|*Experimental (Alpha)*|Shipped but not production-ready; missing critical features; not supported for production workloads.|
|ServerGroup|Nova|*Experimental (Alpha)*|Shipped but not production-ready; missing critical features; not supported for production workloads.|
|Volume|Cinder|*Not Included*|Out of scope for Tech Preview; not yet implemented upstream.|
|LoadBalancer|Octavia|*Not Included*|Out of scope for Tech Preview; not yet implemented upstream.|
|DNS Zone/RecordSet|Designate|*Not Included*|Out of scope for Tech Preview; not yet implemented upstream.|
|Object Storage|Swift|*Not Included*|Out of scope for Tech Preview; not yet implemented upstream.|
|Shared Filesystem|Manila|*Not Included*|Out of scope for Tech Preview; not yet implemented upstream.|

----

h2. 11. Glossary

||Term||Definition||
|ORC|OpenStack Resource Controller — a Kubernetes operator that manages OpenStack resources via CRDs.|
|Tech Preview|A Red Hat release designation indicating the feature is available for testing and feedback but is not fully supported for production workloads.|
|CRD|Custom Resource Definition — a Kubernetes extension mechanism that allows defining new resource types.|
|OLM|Operator Lifecycle Manager — the Red Hat framework for packaging, distributing, and upgrading Kubernetes operators.|
|CAPO|Cluster API Provider OpenStack — a Cluster API implementation that provisions Kubernetes clusters on OpenStack.|
|Drift Detection|The process by which ORC compares the actual state of an OpenStack resource against the declared desired state and reconciles differences.|
|Brownfield Adoption|The ability to import and manage pre-existing OpenStack resources without deleting and recreating them.|
|GitOps|An operational model where infrastructure and application configuration is stored in Git and applied declaratively.|
|v1alpha1|The upstream ORC API version, indicating the API is not yet stable and may change between releases.|

----

items.fromString:
h1. Feature: Remove OCP 4.16 Support from RHOSO 18

[RHOSSTRAT-1302|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOSSTRAT-1302]

h2. Overview

RHOSO 18 currently supports OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) versions including 4.16. Per the [Red Hat OpenStack Platform Life Cycle policy|https://access.redhat.com/support/policy/updates/openstack/platform], RHOSO supports OCP versions within the 2-year Extended Update Support (EUS) Term 1 window; EUS Term 2 and beyond are not supported. OCP 4.16's EUS Term 1 window ends June 27, 2026, after which it falls outside the OCP versions RHOSO is committed to supporting.

This feature removes OCP 4.16 from the RHOSO 18 support matrix beginning with RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6. Customers running RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.16 will no longer receive RHOSO updates after that milestone. Release notes and documentation will guide customers through the upgrade to OCP 4.18 or newer so they can continue receiving RHOSO 18 updates.

By aligning the RHOSO 18 support matrix with Red Hat's OCP lifecycle policy, this feature reduces maintenance burden, simplifies support, and ensures customers are on a supported platform combination.

----

h2. Goals

h3. Technical Objectives

- Remove OCP 4.16 from the RHOSO 18 update graph so customers on OCP 4.16 do not receive RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 or later updates
- Remove OCP 4.16 the OLM bundle
- Publish release notes for RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 documenting that OCP 4.16 is no longer supported and that OCP 4.18 or newer is required for continued updates
- Update the RHOSO 18 support matrix documentation to accurately reflect OCP 4.16 as no longer supported

h3. Who benefits from this Feature, and how?

- *Red Hat Engineering:* Removes the maintenance burden of testing and delivering against an end-of-life OCP version, reducing operational overhead and risk.
- *Documentation & Support Readiness:* Clear release notes and updated support matrix give support engineers and customers unambiguous guidance, reducing the chance of customers landing on an unsupported platform combination.
- *Customers:* Clear release notes and upgrade guidance help customers plan their OCP upgrade ahead of time and avoid gaps in RHOSO update availability.

h3. What is the difference between today's current state and a world with this Feature?

Today, the RHOSO 18 update graph and OLM bundle include OCP 4.16, meaning customers on OCP 4.16 continue to receive RHOSO updates even though OCP 4.16 is no longer under standard maintenance. This results in a platform combination that falls outside the bounds of what Red Hat can fully support, increasing support complexity and diverging from Red Hat's lifecycle commitments.

With this feature in place, customers on OCP 4.16 will not receive RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 or later updates. The update graph will route only to supported OCP versions. Customers will have clear documentation explaining the required upgrade path to OCP 4.18 or newer, and the official RHOSO 18 support matrix will accurately reflect the change.

----

h2. Requirements

|Requirement|Notes|isMVP?|
||OCP 4.16 removed from the RHOSO 18 update graph||Customers on OCP 4.16 must not receive RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 or later updates||Yes||
|OCP 4.16 OLM bundle removed|Bundle must not advertise compatibility with OCP 4.16|Yes|
|Release notes published for RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 documenting the change|Customers must be informed that OCP 4.18 or newer is required|Yes|
|RHOSO 18 support matrix updated to reflect OCP 4.16 as no longer supported|Documentation must accurately reflect the current support matrix|Yes|

----

h2. Done - Acceptance Criteria

This feature is considered complete when:

# Customers running RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.16 no longer receive RHOSO updates starting with 18.0.21 FR6.
# Release notes for RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 are published and clearly state that OCP 4.18 or newer is required to continue receiving RHOSO 18 updates.
# The RHOSO 18 support matrix documentation accurately reflects OCP 4.16 as no longer supported.
# The RHOSO 18 update graph of RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 or later no longer contains OCP 4.16.
# Release notes for RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 explicitly state that an OCP 4.16 EUS entitlement does not extend RHOSO 18 support for OCP 4.16.
# Release notes for RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 include guidance for customers with air-gapped deployments.

----

h2. Use Cases

h3. Customer on OCP 4.16 Attempting to Update RHOSO

A customer running RHOSO 18 on OCP 4.16 checks for available updates after the FR6 milestone. No RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 or later updates are available to them. The release notes they read explain that they must upgrade their OCP cluster to version 4.18 or newer before they can receive further RHOSO 18 updates.

h3. Customer Planning Their Upgrade Path

A customer reads the RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 release notes during release preparation. The notes clearly document that OCP 4.16 support has ended and provide guidance on upgrading to OCP 4.18 or newer. The customer can plan their OCP upgrade before the next RHOSO update window.

h3. Support Engineer Handling a Customer Case

A support engineer receives a case from a customer who is not receiving RHOSO updates. The engineer consults the updated support matrix, identifies that the customer is on OCP 4.16, and uses the documented upgrade path to advise the customer on moving to OCP 4.18 or newer.

----

h2. Out of Scope

- Actively blocking or removing existing RHOSO installations on OCP 4.16 — customers may remain on their current installed version; only new updates are gated
- Any changes to CI or testing environments — CI migration to OCP 4.20-based environments is already handled separately
- Any RHOSO 19 work
- Any changes to OCP 4.17 or other version support

----

h2. Documentation Considerations

The primary documentation deliverable is a release notes entry for RHOSO 18.0.21 FR6 that communicates:

- OCP 4.16 is no longer supported in RHOSO 18 as of 18.0.21 FR6

*Feature Overview*

Currently we ship Horizon in RHOSO with a custom theme, that was designed over a decade ago to match the looks of another Red Hat product that is by now discontinued – the Red Hat CloudForms. While creating such solution was possible thanks to the flexibility of Horizon’s theming system, it comes with ongoing maintenance costs: every non-trivial difference has to be accounted for when back-porting upstream features and bug fixes, writing integration tests, or even just upgrading to newer versions of libraries. We no longer need Horizon to look like CloudForms, but because there never was a decision made to stop using this custom theme, we keep paying the costs.

Examples of the current theme:

!Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-42-59.png|width=1094,alt="Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-42-59.png"!

!Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-40-35.png|width=1094,alt="Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-40-35.png"!

!Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-39-57.png|width=1094,alt="Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-39-57.png"!



We should stop using the current downstream theme, and instead develop a new theme, which introduces Red Hat custom branding and colors without changing the structure or position of the menus, compared to the upstream theme.

Examples of the upstream theme:

!Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-43-33.png|width=1094,alt="Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-43-33.png"!

!Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-44-09.png|width=1094,alt="Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-44-09.png"!

!Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-44-39.png|width=1094,alt="Screenshot_2026-05-12_11-44-39.png"!

A new theme that is more consistent with the upstream OpenStack theme will be easier to maintain, reducing the amount of time needed for development and the opportunity for downstream-only defects that can’t be detected or fixed by the wider community. It will also benefit from usability testing done by the wider community, not just our customers.

It will also make it easier for people already familiar with the upstream OpenStack or offerings from other companies, to switch to the Red Hat version.

Finally, it will be more in line with the OpenShift Console and similar software, as it follows more modern trends in interface design.

Example of the OpenShift Console interface:

items.fromString:
*Initiative Overview* 

The cyborg-tempest-plugin currently lacks comprehensive test coverage,
modern tooling, and structural consistency needed to reliably validate
the OpenStack Cyborg (accelerator management) API and its integration
with Nova instances.

This initiative addresses gaps in test uniqueness, microversion                                                                                                        
support, API coverage, multi-driver scenario testing, hardware CI
infrastructure, and developer experience tooling.                                                                                                                      

The goal is to ensure that Cyborg's full accelerator lifecycle —
devices, deployables, attributes, PCI/NVMe devices, and Nova instance
actions — is continuously exercised by Tempest across all supported
drivers, reducing the risk of regressions and improving confidence                                                                                                     
in Cyborg releases.

*Goals (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
*Who benefits from this Initiative, and how?*

* Cyborg developers gain a reliable, comprehensive test suite
that catches regressions early across all supported drivers, not                                                                                                       
just the fake driver.
* OpenStack CI/CD pipelines benefit from deterministic,                                                                                                                
non-conflicting test runs via stable test IDs, proper microversion
handling, and a new cyborg_features tempest config flag that                                                                                                           
gates hardware-dependent tests.                                                                                                                                        
* Operators and cloud consumers gain higher confidence in Cyborg                                                                                                       
accelerator functionality (PCI/NVMe devices, device profiles,                                                                                                          
instance actions) being continuously validated against both
software simulators and real hardware through third-party CI.                                                                                                          
* New contributors benefit from cleaner code structure (shared                                                                                                         
base classes, consistent exception handling, modern tooling) that                                                                                                      
lowers the onboarding barrier.                                                                                                                                         
* Hardware CI maintainers (e.g., via rdoci or similar) have a
clear, structured set of tests to run against real accelerator                                                                                                         
hardware.                                                                                                                                                              

  *Current state vs. a world with this Initiative*                                                                                                                         

  Today, the cyborg-tempest-plugin has the following problems:                                                                                                           

* Missing stable test IDs, creating a risk of conflicts in parallel runs                                                                                               
* No microversion support
* Incomplete API coverage for attributes, deployables, and device                                                                                                      
operations      
* Only a single scenario test, hardcoded to the fake driver, with no
per-driver equivalent                                                                                                                                                  
* Duplicated base class logic between api/base.py and
scenario/base.py                                                                                                                                                       
* No tempest config flag to control hardware-dependent accelerator tests
* No PCI/NVMe driver test coverage                                                                                                                                     
* No CI infrastructure for hardware testing
* Outdated Python packaging and no code formatting tooling                                                                                                             

  After this initiative, all tests will be uniquely identified and the                                                                                                   
  full Cyborg REST API surface will be covered. Scenario tests will                                                                                                      
  exercise the complete instance-accelerator lifecycle per driver —                                                                                                      
  fake, PCI/NVMe via nvmevirt simulator, and real hardware via                                                                                                           
  third-party CI. Code will be DRY with a shared CommonMixing base                                                                                                       
  class, and a cyborg_features tempest config flag will gate                                                                                                             
  hardware-dependent tests. The project will adopt pyproject.toml                                                                                                        
  and ruff as standard tooling, matching the quality bar set by                                                                                                          
  peer plugins like watcher-tempest-plugin.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      

                                           

*Done - Acceptance Criteria (mandatory* - _Complete while in_ *_Refinement_* _status):_
Detailed task list is captured here: [https://etherpad.opendev.org/p/cyborg-tempest-plugin-improvements|https://etherpad.opendev.org/p/cyborg-tempest-plugin-improvements]

# Stable test IDs

  All tests include a unique stable UUID identifier.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                

# Microversion support

  Tempest tests declare and negotiate Cyborg API microversions,
  consistent with the approach in
  watcher-tempest-plugin/956306.

# API test coverage

  New API tests exist for all of the following, grounded in                                                                                                              
  cyborg_rest_client.py and the
  Cyborg API reference:                                                                                                                                                  

* Create Attribute                                                                                                                                                     
* Delete Attribute                                                                                                                                                     
* Deployables: List, Get
* Devices: List, Get one, Enable, Disable

# CommonMixing base class

  A shared CommonMixing class is introduced (ref:
  watcher-tempest-plugin/967522).
  The create_device_profile method is moved from scenario/base.py                                                                                                        
  into it and consumed by both api/base.py and scenario/base.py.                                                                                                         

# Exception review                                                                                                                                                    

  All exceptions used in test code are reviewed and use appropriate                                                                                                      
  Tempest/Cyborg exception types with no bare except blocks or
  inconsistent patterns.                                                                                                                                                 

# Per-driver scenario tests

  The single fake-driver scenario test is refactored into a
  driver-agnostic base. Equivalent scenario tests exist for each
  supported driver. Instance action scenario tests cover:                                                                                                                
  Pause/Unpause, Backup, Snapshot, Lock/Unlock, Rebuild,
  Shelve/Unshelve — validated first with the fake driver against the                                                                                                     
  Cyborg support matrix,
  then with real driver equivalents.                                                                                                                                     

# oslo.log logging                                                                                                                                                    

  Structured logging via oslo.log is introduced in all scenario                                                                                                          
  tests.

# PCI/NVMe driver testing

  Scenario tests for the PCI/NVMe driver are implemented. The nvmevirt
  simulator driver is the preferred path. If not viable, a third-party
  CI pipeline (via rdoci or equivalent) is established with the                                                                                                          
  following CI environment requirements validated and documented:                                                                                                        

* VM with vIOMMU enabled                                                                                                                                               
* UEFI boot (non-secure boot) with q35 machine type

# cyborg_features tempest config flag                                                                                                                                 

  A new tempest config option (group: cyborg_features or equivalent)                                                                                                     
  is introduced to gate accelerator-hardware-dependent tests. The
  design — single boolean vs. per-operation flags — is decided during
  code review and documented in the config reference.                                                                                                                    

# Whitebox tests                                                                                                                                                     

  A whitebox-tempest-plugin test exists for NVMe devices that
  SSH-writes data to the device, unbinds it, and asserts the device
  is cleaned after unbind.                                                                                                                                               

# Modern tooling                                                                                                                                                     

* Project is migrated from setup.cfg/setup.py to pyproject.toml                                                                                                        
* ruff is introduced for linting and formatting, integrated into
tox and pre-commit                                               

*Out of Scope _* __(Initial completion while in_ *_Refinement_* _status):_
High-level list of items or persona’s that are out of scope.
<your text here>

* …

items.fromString:
h2. Feature Overview

CloudKitty's Loki storage backend now supports structured metadata and per-project stream partitioning, significantly improving query performance for chargeback data retrieval. A new configuration option ({{use_structured_metadata}}) allows operators to enable indexed metadata filtering after upgrading, replacing the previous approach of parsing unstructured JSON on every query.

h2. Goals

* Operators running chargeback at scale benefit from dramatically faster Loki queries by leveraging indexed metadata filtering instead of full JSON parsing.
* Today, all chargeback dataframes are stored as unstructured JSON in a single Loki stream, requiring every query to scan all dataframes across all projects. With this feature, data is partitioned per project and commonly queried fields are stored as indexed metadata, reducing query scope and improving retrieval time.

h2. Requirements

||Requirement||Notes||isMVP?||
|Store structured metadata with each Loki log entry for fields: type, user, unit, flavor_name|Always stored regardless of config setting|Yes|
|Partition Loki streams by project_id|Streams keyed as {{\{service="cloudkitty", project_id="..."\}}}|Yes|
|Add {{use_structured_metadata}} config option under {{[storage_loki]}}|Default: false, requires Loki 3.0+|Yes|
|Enforce 5000-element query limit with user-facing error|Loki silently fails above this limit; CloudKitty must surface the error|Yes|
|Backward compatibility when {{use_structured_metadata=false}}|Existing JSON parsing behavior preserved|Yes|

h2. Done - Acceptance Criteria

* Structured metadata is stored automatically with every new Loki log entry for the indexed fields (type, user, unit, flavor_name).
* When {{use_structured_metadata=true}}, CloudKitty queries filter on indexed metadata rather than parsing JSON, resulting in measurable query performance improvement.
* When {{use_structured_metadata=false}} (default), existing query behavior is unchanged - backward compatible.
* Loki streams are partitioned by project_id for improved query scoping and scalability.
* Queries exceeding 5000 elements return a clear error to the user rather than failing silently.

h2. Use Cases

# *Upgrade path:* Operator upgrades CloudKitty to the new version. Structured metadata is stored automatically. After the data retention period passes (old data without metadata expires), operator sets {{use_structured_metadata=true}} in {{[storage_loki]}} config. Queries now use fast indexed filtering.
# *Multi-tenant scale:* In a deployment with many OpenStack projects, queries for a single project's chargeback data no longer scan all projects' dataframes - each project has its own Loki stream.
# *Large result sets:* When a query would return more than 5000 dataframes, the user receives a clear error message instead of silent data truncation.

h2. Out of Scope

* Changes to non-Loki storage backends.
* Automatic migration of existing data to structured metadata format (relies on retention-based expiry).
* Loki deployment or version upgrade procedures.

h2. Documentation Considerations

* New configuration option {{use_structured_metadata}} under {{[storage_loki]}} must be documented with the migration path (deploy, wait for retention, enable).
* Loki 3.0+ version requirement must be noted.
* The 5000-element query limit should be documented as a known constraint.
* Upstream docs updated: {{doc/source/admin/configuration/storage.rst}}.

h2. Questions to Answer

* What is the expected data retention period customers should wait before enabling {{use_structured_metadata}}?
* Does the RHOSO Loki deployment already meet the Loki 3.0+ requirement?
* Should the 5000-element limit be configurable or is it a fixed Loki constraint?

h2. Background and Strategic Fit

This feature is a follow-on to the Chargeback GA delivery (RHOSSTRAT-1006). As chargeback adoption grows, query performance against Loki becomes critical for production-scale deployments. This work ensures the storage backend scales efficiently with the number of projects and volume of chargeback data.

h2. Customer Considerations

* This is an opt-in performance optimization - no customer action required on upgrade, but customers should be made aware of the new config option to realize the performance benefits.
* Customers must be running Loki 3.0+ to enable structured metadata filtering.
* The migration path is non-disruptive: new data automatically includes metadata, and the feature can be enabled once old data expires.

items.fromString:
*Initiative Overview*
The OpenStackVersion minor update process currently executes 8 sequential steps automatically once a new targetVersion is set. While the sequencing enforces ordering (each step blocks on the previous), there is no mechanism for an operator/administrator to pause between steps, gate progression, or manually approve advancement to the next stage. This epic introduces a annotation-based mechanism on the OpenStackVersion resource that allows administrators to manually control progression through individual minor update steps.

*Goals* 
Introduce a single annotation-based gating mechanism on the OpenStackVersion resource. The annotation value names the furthest update stage the controller is allowed to reach before pausing. Once the controller completes the named stage it stops and waits. To advance, the administrator either updates the annotation value to the next stage name, or removes the annotation entirely to allow the update to run to completion.

 This approach is consistent with the existing [core.openstack.org/deploym|http://core.openstack.org/deploym] ent-stage annotation already used on the ControlPlane resource.

*Done - Acceptance Criteria*

* The gate annotation on OpenStackVersion prevents the controller from advancing past the named stage.

* Updating the annotation value or removing it allows the controller to proceed on the next reconciliation.

* The update process remains fully automatic when no annotation is present (backward compatibility).

* The annotation only affects the update workflow, not default reconciliation.

* Condition status/reason/message clearly indicates when a stage is gated vs. in-progress vs. completed.

* The annotation can be applied before initiating the update (pre-staging).

* Documentation and examples are provided for common gating workflows.                                            



*Out of Scope*
Some steps in the minor update process already have implicit manual controls (e.g., the dataplane step requires the administrator to create an OpenStackDataPlaneDeployment CR).

*Initiative Overview*

The RHOSO partner certification program is owned by an external team, but this initiative will track the delivery. The test harness content delivery and process are owned by rh-cert, but RHOS engineering owns the code development and maintenance.  For RHOSO-19, we need to ensure a working version is consumable by partners in Beta as part of the Early Access program and we have a timely release of the official RHOSO-19 version so that partners can quickly re-run certification on the GA release and make their solutions available to RHOSO-19 customers that depend on vendor-based storage and networking solutions.

*Done - Acceptance Criteria*

* Beta delivers a working rhos-cert version with MVP of updates to latest upstream tempest tests as needed for Storage and Networking
* GA delivers rhos-cert with all tests that are scoped for RHOS 19 certification needs

*Out of Scope* 

* Any cert policy requests or needs for RHOS 19

items.toString:
Title: Add OpenStackAssistant CRD to deploy an AI agent pod for cluster diagnostics

Type: Feature

Summary:
This feature will be added to the openstack-operator

Introduce a new OpenStackAssistant CRD ([assistant.openstack.org/v1beta1|http://assistant.openstack.org/v1beta1]) that deploys a managed AI agent pod into the OpenStack control plane namespace. The initial implementation uses Goose ([http://github.com/block/goose|http://github.com/block/goose|smart-link] ) as the AI agent runtime, with a provider-based abstraction to support additional agent runtimes in the future.

Description:

h2. Problem

Operators managing OpenStack on OpenShift currently lack an automated, in-cluster AI assistant for diagnosing cluster health issues. Running diagnostic tooling today requires manually launching a Goose container via Podman on a workstation, copying in a kubeconfig, configuring TLS certificates, and managing provider credentials by hand. This is error-prone and not reproducible across environments.

h2. Proposed Solution

Add a new CRD called OpenStackAssistant that automates the deployment of an AI agent pod with proper RBAC and configuration. The operator creates and manages:

* A _ServiceAccount_ with a locked-down, read-only Role/RoleBinding scoped to the OpenStack namespace (pods, services, configmaps, secrets, events, all [http://openstack.org|http://openstack.org|smart-link]  CRDs, routes, network-attachment-definitions, etc.)
* A _ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding_ granting read-only access to cluster-scoped resources needed for diagnostics (nodes, persistentvolumes, clusteroperators, clusterversions, nodenetworkconfigurationpolicies, events across all namespaces, storageclasses, machines)
* A _ConfigMap_ containing the generated entrypoint script that configures the agent at pod startup
* A _Pod_ running the AI agent container (e.g., Goose with oc/kubectl installed), using the ServiceAccount token for in-cluster Kubernetes API access

h2. Key Design Decisions

_Provider abstraction:_ The CRD includes a {{provider}} field (enum, defaulting to "goose") so that future AI agent runtimes can be added without CRD schema changes to common fields. Provider-specific configuration (extensions, config file format) is encapsulated in the entrypoint script and container image.

_Lightspeed Stack backend:_ The AI agent communicates with a Lightspeed Stack deployment for LLM inference. The backend may run on the same OCP cluster or on a separate cluster. All connectivity details (base URL, API key, model, custom headers) are encapsulated in a user-provided Secret, so the CRD does not need to distinguish between same-cluster and cross-cluster deployments. An optional CA bundle Secret supports custom TLS certificates.

_Read-only RBAC:_ The assistant pod is strictly read-only. Write operations (edit, patch, delete) are denied by the RBAC rules. This is enforced at the Kubernetes API level via the ServiceAccount permissions, not just by agent configuration.

_In-cluster auth:_ The pod uses the automatically mounted ServiceAccount token for Kubernetes API access. No external kubeconfig file is needed. The oc/kubectl CLI tools auto-detect the in-cluster credentials.

_Finalizer for cluster-scoped cleanup:_ Since ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding cannot use owner references (they are cluster-scoped while the CR is namespaced), a finalizer ensures these resources are cleaned up when the CR is deleted.

h2. CRD Spec Fields

* {{containerImage}} (required) - Container image with the AI agent and oc/kubectl installed
* {{provider}} (optional, default: "goose") - AI agent provider type
* {{lightspeedStack.providerSecret}} (required) - Secret containing the provider config JSON
* {{lightspeedStack.caBundleSecretName}} (optional) - Secret with CA certs for TLS
* {{recipes}} (optional) - ConfigMap with recipe YAML files (slash commands like /cluster-health)
* {{gooseHints}} (optional) - ConfigMap with .goosehints context file
* {{nodeSelector}} (optional) - Node scheduling constraints
* {{env}} (optional) - Additional environment variables (GOOSE_MODEL, LIGHTSPEED_API_KEY, etc.)

h2. User Workflow

User creates prerequisite Secrets and ConfigMaps (provider config, recipes, hints)

User creates an OpenStackAssistant CR

Operator reconciles: creates SA, Role, RoleBinding, ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, ConfigMap, Pod

User connects: {{oc exec -it <pod> -n openstack -- goose session}}

User runs diagnostic recipes: {{/cluster-health}}

Goose queries the cluster via oc using the ServiceAccount token and generates reports

h2. Scope

* Scaffold the API and controller using operator-sdk
* Implement the full reconciler following the existing OpenStackClient controller pattern
* Leverage existing internal/openstackassistant/funcs.go (EntrypointScript, AssistantPodSpec)
* Wire up the controller in cmd/main.go

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* OpenStackAssistant CR can be created and reconciles to a running pod
* All RBAC resources (SA, Role, RoleBinding, ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding) are created with correct read-only permissions
* Pod can execute read-only oc commands (oc get nodes, oc get pods, oc get clusteroperators)
* Pod cannot execute write commands (oc delete, oc patch)
* Goose session starts successfully inside the pod and can run the /cluster-health recipe
* Deleting the CR cleans up all resources including cluster-scoped ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding
* Status conditions accurately reflect the state of all sub-resources

items.fromString:
h2. Summary

This initiative presents the *Agentic AI pilot* for our team. We will select and develop an *Agentic AI–based workflow* to *automate the SDLC*, aligned with the company *Q2 strategy* to prioritize *AI-first* implementation in our development cycles.

h2. Scope

* Select an Agentic AI–based workflow appropriate for our toolchain and processes.
* Design and implement the workflow to automate parts of the SDLC (discovery through delivery as agreed by the team).
* Integrate the necessary tools to support the pilot end-to-end.

h2. 60-day POC

The team will run a *60-day proof of concept* to demonstrate:

* Benefits of applying Agentic AI within our specific development processes.
* Challenges, constraints, and lessons learned (technical, process, and organizational).

h2. Success criteria (initial)

* A working integrated workflow demonstrable within the POC window.
* Documented outcomes: advantages, challenges, and recommendations for next steps.

h2. Alignment

Supports Q2 company focus on *AI-first* development practices.
items.toString:
h1. Initiative Overview

This initiative presents the Agentic AI pilot for our team. We will select and develop an Agentic AI–based workflow to automate the SDLC, aligned with the company Q2 strategy to prioritize AI-first implementation in our development cycles. This supports the Q2 company focus on AI-first development practices.

h1. Goals

The team will run a 60-day proof of concept to demonstrate:

* Benefits of applying Agentic AI within our specific development processes.
* Challenges, constraints, and lessons learned (technical, process, and organizational).

h1. Acceptance Criteria

* Select an Agentic AI–based workflow appropriate for our toolchain and processes.
* Design and implement the workflow to automate parts of the SDLC (discovery through delivery as agreed by the team).
* Integrate the necessary tools to support the pilot end-to-end.
* A working integrated workflow demonstrable within the POC window.
* Documented outcomes: advantages, challenges, and recommendations for next steps.

h1. Out of Scope

* *Full Production Rollout:* Implementing the workflow as a permanent, department-wide standard is excluded from this 60-day pilot phase.
* *Proprietary Model Development:* Building or fine-tuning custom LLMs from scratch; the focus is on Agentic orchestration and integration of existing tools.
* *Legacy System Modernization:* Automation of manual processes within legacy toolchains that are not part of the current prioritized SDLC.
* *External Team Training:* Comprehensive onboarding or documentation for teams not directly participating in the pilot.

items.toString:
*Initiative Overview*

AMD's MI300X GPUs now support multiple Virtual Functions (VFs) per physical GPU through the open-source GIM driver (8.4.1+), enabling 8 VFs per GPU with potential scaling to 64 VFs through advanced partitioning. Currently it has been verified that RHOSO supports 1 vGPU per physical GPU for SR-IOV-capable GPUs. This initiative aims to enable OpenStack Nova integration for multi-VF GPU partitioning to support a Tier 1 strategic account requiring production-scale AI/ML workloads with GPU resource optimization.

AMD has successfully demonstrated 64 VF configurations at the KVM/ROCm level on bare metal and requires OpenStack integration to enable multi-VF passthrough to multiple VMs. This work is critical for the joint customer POC progression and represents a collaborative effort between Red Hat and AMD, where Red Hat owns integration (RHEL, KVM, libvirt, Nova, RHOSO) and AMD owns the GIM driver support.


*Goals*

* *Phase 0*: HW preparation and RHOSO deployment validation
** Verify the provided HW for verification and validate basic functionality of deployed RHOSO
* *Phase 1*: 8 VF Support (Minimum Viable Product)
** Enable Nova to discover and inventory up to 8 VFs per MI300X GPU exposed by AMD GIM driver 8.4.1+
** Validate Nova scheduler capability to correctly discover and inventory VFs exposed by the GIM driver and allocate individual VFs to different VMs (1 VF per VM, multiple VMs sharing the same physical GPU)
** Support flavor extra specs to request specific number of VFs (e.g., resources:vGPU=2) with optional hints for same/different GPU placement
** Validate NUMA affinity awareness when allocating multiple VFs to ensure optimal performance
* *Phase 2*: NUMA & Scale Validation
** Validate VF scheduling across multiple GPUs in large-scale environments (e.g., 8-GPU systems)
** Conduct performance benchmarking with ROCm workloads to ensure parity with bare-metal performance
** Execute interconnect isolation testing to confirm VF isolation across different partitions
* *Phase 3*: 64 VF Support (Advanced Partitioning)
** Enable use cases where a single VM can consume multiple VFs from the same GPU
** Validate with AMD that GIM driver correctly exposes 64 VFs and mediated device creation works at scale


*Phase 0 Acceptance Criteria*

* Establish communication channels between teams
* Investigate location of the lab instances which will be provided for validation 
* Create jumphost for lab connection, provide ssh keys to AMD team
* Validation of provided HW by AMD team
* Validation of deployed RHOSO instance and provide guidance to AMD team to mitigate any issues

*Phase 1 Acceptance Criteria*

* Verification of Nova successfully discovers 8 VFs per MI300X GPU on systems with AMD GIM driver 8.4.1+
* Verification of Nova scheduler allocates individual VFs to different VMs without conflicts
* Verification of Flavor extra specs correctly request and allocate specified number of VFs
* Verification of NUMA affinity is respected during VF allocation (VFs from different GPUs on same NUMA node or per operator policy)
* Internal documentation published covering installation, configuration, and usage patterns
* QE validates basic multi-VF allocation scenarios (2 VMs, 4 VMs, 8 VMs on single GPU)

*Phase 2 Acceptance Criteria*

* Multi-GPU VF scheduling validated on 8-GPU systems
* Scheduler demonstrates balanced VF distribution across available GPUs
* Performance benchmarks show <5% degradation vs. bare-metal ROCm workloads
* Interconnect isolation tests confirm no interference between VFs from different partitions
* Scale testing with multiple concurrent VMs demonstrates stable operation

*Phase 3 Acceptance Criteria*

* 64 VF topology documented and understood
* Verification of Nova scheduler handles 64 VFs from single GPU (without code changes)
* Verification of Single VM can consume multiple VFs from same GPU
* AMD confirms GIM driver 64 VF support and mediated device creation at scale
* End-to-end validation with customer workloads


*Dependencies that need to be resolved*

* AMD provides dedicated MI300X hardware for Red Hat engineering validation
* AMD engineering provides driver bug fix support and escalation path during validation
* AMD engineering provides GIM driver installation and RHOSO deployment on provided nodes


*Out of Scope*

* Support for non-MI300X AMD GPUs in this initiative (may be addressed separately based on customer demand)
* vGPU live migration (existing RHOSO limitation applies; future enhancement potential)
* Dynamic VF count adjustment after GPU initialization (requires GIM driver reinitialization)
* Multi-tenancy security isolation beyond what AMD GIM driver provides (driver-level responsibility)
* GPU memory overcommitment or time-slicing (not supported by SR-IOV architecture)
* Performance optimization of ROCm workloads themselves (customer/AMD responsibility)
* GIM driver installation is out of scope of the documentation as this stays on customer side responsibility
* Any scheduler improvements (if needed) to balance VF allocations and avoid resource fragmentation. Any necessary implementation change will be formed into RFE.


*Open questions*

* Feasibility of S64 VF on 8 GPUs: Does Nova require code changes to support 64 independent VFs from one GPU? Initial community discussions suggest scheduler may handle it, but validation required
* Multi-VF to single VM: Performance benefit analysis for multiple VFs from same GPU to one VM vs. licensing/partitioning artifact (AMD to clarify)
* Documentation ownership: Determine if this will be new RHOSO guide section or AMD-specific knowledge base article
* Hardware access strategy: Short-term vs. long-term access to MI300X hardware for Red Hat engineering and QE teams (to be discussed with AMD)
This work item is caused by RHOSRFE-332

Enhanced CADF-compliant audit logging across OpenStack services::
+
--
With this update, the RHOSO logging architecture is enhanced to activate CADF-compliant audit logging across OpenStack services. This separation of security events from operational noise will improve the end user's experience by simplifying compliance processes, meeting regulatory standards more effectively, and laying the groundwork for the inclusion of other core services. The goal is to strengthen RHOSO's security posture, particularly for government and regulated customers, by meeting strict regulatory standards and enabling independent routing of security events for Keystone.

items.toString:
h3. Feature Overview



This feature strengthens the RHOSO logging architecture by enabling the existing control plane service “Audit" stream. By leveraging existing logging interfaces, we are building a specialized pipeline that identifies and tags OpenStack CADF (Cloud Auditing Data Federation) event notifications and allows them to be forwarded to an alternative destination. This separation allows RHOSO to meet strict regulatory standards by enabling independent routing of security events for Keystone (MVP) and lays the groundwork for other core services.

h3. Goals

*High-level Goal:* Activate CADF-compliant audit logging across OpenStack services and implement filters to route these security events to external destinations.

Who benefits and how?

* Security & Compliance Teams: Can prove "Chain of Custody" and meet data sovereignty/audit laws without manual log filtering.
* Government/Regulated Customers: Unblocks adoption for agencies requiring strict separation of operational and security data.

Difference between today’s state and a world with this Feature:

* Current: Audit events are buried in "Application" logs; proving compliance is manual and error-prone.
* Future: OpenStack audit events are enabled, identified via filters, and can be forwarded.

h3. Requirements

|*Requirement*|*Notes*|*isMVP?*|
|*Tag Keystone Events as Audit*|Capture Keystone CADF event notifications and label them as "Audit" type.|Yes|
|*Log Forwarding*|Ensure "Audit" tagged logs can be routed to external targets (separate from App/Infra logs)|Yes|
|*CADF Formatted Logs*|Structured logs to simplify analysis in SIEM tools.|Yes|
|*Tag Additional Services*|Enable audit events from Nova, Barbican, Glance, Cinder, and Neutron (per RFE requirements).|No|

h3. Done - Acceptance Criteria

Value Proposition: Compliance teams can isolate security events from operational noise to satisfy regulatory audits.

Scope & Outcome:

* Keystone CADF events are successfully identified as "Audit" type logs.
* Configuration allows forwarding _only_ Audit logs to a specific external endpoint.
* Operational logs (debug/info) remain in their defined logging domains.

h3. Use Cases - i.e. User Experience & Workflow

* Regulatory Compliance: A government admin configures the system to forward all "Audit" logs to a secure, immutable storage bucket to meet sovereignty laws, while keeping debug logs local for troubleshooting.
* Security Monitoring: An analyst connects a SIEM to the audit storage bucket to detect unauthorized access attempts (Keystone) without consuming license quota on high-volume infrastructure logs.

h3. Out of Scope

* SIEM tool integration after audit logs are identified and forwarded.
* Extending the current audit log features within the OpenStack services, such as the creation of new audit logs.
* _Enablement of dataplane audit logs. The feature is focused on the control plane._

h3. Documentation Considerations

* Configuration guide for splitting Audit streams from other logs and forwarding using existing OpenShift Logging interfaces..
* Enablement of audit logging for the OpenStack services that have it available.

h3. Questions to Answer

* Can events tagged as audit be selected/customized by the cluster admin.

h3. Background and Strategic Fit

* _Direct Customer Driver_: A customer is blocked from deploying RHOSO 18 due to lack of audit log separation (Request for Enhancement: CADF Audit Logs).
* _Strategic Value_: Essential for Public Sector and Financial Services adoption.
* Spike: [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSPRH-22255|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSPRH-22255|smart-link] 

h3. Customer Considerations

* _Tamper Resistance_: The separation mechanism must be robust enough to pass government security audits.
* _Expansion_: While Keystone is MVP, the customer eventually requires the full suite (Nova, Barbican, Cinder, Glance, Neutron) for production.

items.toString:
*Feature Overview (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
_In our current deployment, we route all the traffic to the central keystone from the workload domains through the public endpoint of the central region. There is therefore no separation between public keystone requests and requests from services in the workload regions._

This opens up the possibility of a DDOS attack, which would be even more catastrophic because it would degrade all the workload regions as well.

In our deployment, we use a technology called skupper (Red Hat Interconnect) to link the barbican-keystone-listener to the rabbitmq instance in the central region.  This provides a separate endpoint for the traffic, which could potentially be secured in some way by the deployer.

We should use this as well for traffic to the keystone internal endpoint.  Note that we expect this to be essentially a documentation fix.  No new code is needed (other than for CI).

*Goals (mandatory -* _Complete while in_ *_New_* _status)_
_Provide high-level goal statement, providing user context and expected user outcome(s) for this Feature_

* Deployers will be able to configure a SKMO environment where traffic to the keystone internal endpoint is directed through a separate endpoint.   There are many ways a customer could do this.  We will document doing this through skupper (Red Hat InterConnect), which is how we already document exposing the central region rabbitmq to the barbican keystone listener.

Content added to Hardening guide for Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift::
The _Hardening a Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift deployment_ guide includes expanded security hardening content that was previously available in the Red Hat OpenStack Platform 17.1 hardening guide. This phase 2 expansion adds guidance for securing endpoints and managing security policies, hardening infrastructure and virtualization, intrusion detection with AIDE, hardening the Dashboard service (horizon), hardening Block Storage (cinder), Shared File Systems (manila), and Object Storage (swift) services, monitoring and logging security events, auditing system  events, messaging transport security, and managing instance security. All hardening instructions have been verified for the RHOSO 18.0 deployment model. For more information, see link:https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openstack_services_on_openshift/18.0/html-single/hardening_a_red_hat_openstack_services_on_openshift_deployment/index[Hardening a Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift deployment].

items.toString: Implement PodRemediator for stateful PVC remediation

items.fromString: PodRemediator: stateful PVC remediation with NHC/SNR
Red Hat OpenStack Services on OpenShift

*Goal*

Provide a controller (PodRemediator) in the infra-operator that integrates with Node Health Check (NHC) and Self Node Remediation (SNR) to remediate pods with local PVCs when worker nodes are marked unhealthy. This implements the direction investigated in OSPRH-14880 and improves cluster resilience for stateful workloads (e.g. Galera, RabbitMQ) on LVMS or local storage.

*Acceptance Criteria*
 * PodRemediator CRD, RBAC (nodes, PVCs, NHC/SNR APIs), and controller logic are implemented in infra-operator; PodRemediator CR is available and the controller runs in the openstack-operators namespace.
 * Controller reaches Ready=True when NHC and SNR are installed and the supplemental RBAC is applied.
 * POC can be reproduced from zero: deploy custom infra-operator image, apply CRD/RBAC, install NHC/SNR, create PodRemediator CR; optional local-PVC test can be applied and verified on the POC cluster
 * Any behavior is documented and aligned with operator expectations (e.g. Galera, RabbitMQ) regarding storage recovery and pod rescheduling; no changes inside mariadb-operator or rabbitmq-cluster-operator are required for this Epic.

References
 * Parent Epic: OSPRH-14880 (Handling non-graceful worker node shutdowns: SNR/NHC behavior and PVCs cleanup on LVMS with Galera & RabbitMQ).
 * Slack discussion and design docs:

items.fromString:
*Initiative Overview*

Based on the [customer’s datacenter design|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1l2Aa-XnyROFmoSsQznjfjPnuCaA5YQRfya1pt-3XSVw/edit?slide=id.g39360f7bfe9_0_8#slide=id.g39360f7bfe9_0_8] and evaluation of Red Hat OpenStack (RHOSO) as the NVIDIA GPU-based virtualization platform for AI workloads. Customer's platform is based on Intel Xeon 6 (Granite Rapids). To be precise: liquid-cooled XE9780L: Intel Granite Rapids-AP: Intel Xeon 6 Performance 69xxP (Socket: LGA7529, Max TDP=500W) air-cooled XE9780: Intel Granite Rapids-SP: Intel Xeon 6 Performance 67xxP (Socket: LGA4710, Max TDP=350W)

Customer requires to verify and validate functionality of specific accelerator features on specific sets of hardware. The customer is evaluating OpenStack and OpenShift Virtualization based platform and needs a clear statement of what is achievable in OpenStack, what requires engineering work, and realistic timelines.

This initiative covers validation on cloud nodes with NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs. The main focus for this initiative is to validate GPU passthrough in RHOSO on such GPU hardware.

There are strict requirements for multi-tenancy including network isolation as well as NVLink multi-tenancy requirements. To ensure isolation of NVLink traffic between different tenants the plan is to use the [NVIDIA Fabric Manager|https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/fabric-manager-user-guide/index.html#virtualization-models]. Validation of GPU passthrough and NVLink multi-tenancy has been completed for NVIDIA HGX H100 GPUs from the RHEL point of view. The similar validation is being requested with the NVIDIA HGX B300 8-GPU NVLink/NVSwitch-based platform with verification of functionality within the RHOSO platform focusing on single-node GPU pooling.
 
*Goals*
 * *Verification of GPU PCI passthrough functionality in RHOSO:* 
 ** Customer needs to be able to PCI passthrough GPUs via Nova Placement to VMs within RHOSO.
 ** {*}Key questions{*}:
 *** Can RHOSO support HGX B300 GPU passthrough with Fabric Manager running locally on the compute node and managing the NVSwitch/NVLink configuration independently of OpenStack?
 *** Are additional Nova, Placement or Cyborg changes required?
 *** Is NVLink currently treated as a single PCI group, and if so, what work is required to support NVLink partitioning/isolation between VMs?

 * *Verification of NVLink multitenancy in RHOSO:* 
 ** Customer needs to be ensured that NVLink multi-tenancy is working properly 
 ** {*}Key questions{*}:
 *** What options exist (or are feasible) to prevent full NVLink coherence across VMs?
 **** PCI grouping changes?
 **** Fabric Manager policy integration?
 **** Explicit constraints / documented limitations?
 *** What is achievable without large upstream changes vs what requires upstream Nova/Cyborg design work?

 * *Documentation:* Documentation of required manual configuration on the dataplane host is needed. Detailed description of issues is expected in case it is discovered during the testing phase that any functionality is missing.

 

{*}D{*}{*}one - Acceptance Criteria{*}{*}:{*}

*Deliverable 1 - Functional Enablement Validation*
 # GPU Assignment
 ## Confirm successful GPU passthrough on HGX B300.
 ## Ensure virtual machines boot correctly with assigned GPU(s).
 ## Check that NVIDIA drivers load properly inside the guest OS.
 # NVLink Multi-Tenancy (Static Model)
 ## Verify Fabric Manager is running on the host.
 ## Confirm implementation of the static NVSwitch partition model.
 ## Ensure GPUs are grouped into tenant-isolated partitions
 ## Test that the Nova scheduler assigns GPU groups to VMs as expected
 ## Validate that VM lifecycle operations (start, stop, reboot, delete) work correctly with these partitions
 # Isolation Validation
 ## Confirm that GPUs assigned to different VMs do not establish NVLink coherence across partitions
 ## Validate VM-to-VM isolation at the NVLink fabric level
 # Stability Validation
 ## Check that partition persistence is maintained through:
 ## Host reboot
 ## VM restart- Ensure there are no device detachment issues during lifecycle events

*Deliverable 2 - Documentation Package* 
 # Host Setup Guide
 ## Ex BIOS settings, Kernel parameter requirements
 ## How to install and configure Fabric Manager
 # NVSwitch Partition Configuration Guide
 ## How to create NVSwitch partitions- Defining GPU groups for each tenant
 ## The relationship between partitions and PCIe devices- How Nova uses GPU groups
 ## Examples for flavor, aggregate, and placement mapping, Example VM launches
 # Troubleshooting Guide
 ## Document any issues discovered during verification process
 # Known Limitations
 ## Ex: GPU and NIC grouping is not available in Phase 1
 ## Dynamic NVSwitch re-partitioning is not supported
 ## No topology-aware scheduling

*Deliverable 3 - Basic Performance & Isolation Validation*
 # Run NCCL bandwidth tests within each partition
 # Use CUDA bandwidth tests to check data transfer inside partitions
 # Test isolation between VMs across different partitions
 # Check the stability of VMs during long-running workloads via standard multi-GPU validation workloads such as NVIDIA NCCL tests (e.g. all_reduce_perf), which actively use NVLink/NVSwitch communication
 # Confirm partitions and configurations persist after host reboots

 
{*}O{*}{*}ut of Scope:{*}
 * This initiative is strictly for purpose of verification of capabilities of currently available components within RHOSO-18.0 and no implementation work is expected.

 * Performance tests are intended solely for infrastructure validation, not for marketing benchmarks
 * This is requested as one time validation before datacenter deployment and does not require recurrent CI job

*Initiative Overview*

Based on the [customer’s datacenter design|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1l2Aa-XnyROFmoSsQznjfjPnuCaA5YQRfya1pt-3XSVw/edit?slide=id.g39360f7bfe9_0_8#slide=id.g39360f7bfe9_0_8] and evaluation of Red Hat OpenStack (RHOSO) as the NVIDIA GPU-based virtualization platform for AI workloads. Customer's platform is based on Intel Xeon 6 (Granite Rapids). To be precise: liquid-cooled XE9780L: Intel Granite Rapids-AP: Intel Xeon 6 Performance 69xxP (Socket: LGA7529, Max TDP=500W) air-cooled XE9780: Intel Granite Rapids-SP: Intel Xeon 6 Performance 67xxP (Socket: LGA4710, Max TDP=350W)

Customer requires to verify and validate functionality of specific accelerator features on specific sets of hardware. The customer is evaluating OpenStack and OpenShift Virtualization based platform and needs a clear statement of what is achievable in OpenStack, what requires engineering work, and realistic timelines.

This initiative covers validation on cloud nodes with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. The main focus for this initiative is to validate vGPU functionality in RHOSO on such GPU hardware for standard enterprise virtualization use cases.

 

*Goals*
 * *Verification of GPU PCI passthrough functionality in RHOSO:* Customer needs to be able to PCI passthrough GPUs via Nova Placement to VMs within RHOSO.

 * *Verification of vGPU functionality in RHOSO:* Customer needs to be able to allocate vGPUs via Nova Placement to VMs within RHOSO. The goal is to divide physical GPU to vGPUs via manual configuration and verify that it is possible to use those vGPUs in Nova managed VM instances. 

 * *Documentation:* Documentation of required manual configuration on the dataplane host is needed. Detailed description of issues is expected in case it is discovered during the testing phase that any functionality is missing.

 # GPU Assignment
 ## Confirm successful GPU passthrough on RTX PRO 6000.
